The climate report tries to reconcile satellite readings with data from ocean buoys that have drifted hundreds of miles since 2019.
Two cousins who had not spoken since the funeral were finally reconciled over a group chat about selling the family cabin.
The treasurer spent Sunday night reconciling the club's bank statement against forty crumpled receipts from the spring fundraiser.
After three rejected appeals she reconciled herself to renting, and started looking at apartments near the train instead of houses.
words.etymology: re-(重新) + conciliare(使联合) → 重新走到一起

meanings.en: the feeling of not belonging to, or not being understood by, the group or society around you
meanings.zh: 疏离感,格格不入的感觉

meanings.en: the act of making someone stop being friendly or loyal to a person or group

examples: Six months of remote onboarding left the new analyst with a quiet alienation that no amount of virtual coffee chats could fix.
The novel treats teenage alienation less as rebellion than as a bus ride home where nobody looks up from their phone.
Sociologists blame the district's rising alienation on the closure of the library, the pool, and the only late-night bus route.
Her lawyer argued that the constant late-night texts amounted to a deliberate alienation of the children from their father.
The manager's habit of rewriting every draft produced a slow alienation of the three writers who had been there longest.
words.etymology: alien-(外人的) + -ation(状态) → 成为局外人的状态

meanings.en: so confusing, strange, or full of choices that you cannot understand it or decide what to do
meanings.zh: 令人困惑的,令人不知所措的

examples: The pharmacy aisle offers a bewildering row of cough syrups that differ only in flavor, price, and the color of the box.
Tokyo's Shinjuku station is bewildering on a first visit; even the signs pointing to the exits seem to disagree with each other.
Her new insurance plan came with a bewildering forty-page glossary that explained one unfamiliar term using three others.
The startup's pricing page was bewilderingly vague, so half the callers to support just wanted to know what a seat cost.
The museum hung the paintings in a bewildering order, so visitors kept circling back to check whether they had missed a room.
words.etymology: be-(使) + wilder(迷失荒野) → 使人如入荒野般困惑

meanings.en: to confuse someone completely, especially by being too complicated or too strange to follow

examples: The new ticketing app bewilders older riders who just want a paper pass and a machine that takes coins.
It still bewilders me that the express train skips my station on Sundays but stops at the empty one two miles north.
The professor bewildered the class by opening with a joke in Latin and refusing to explain it until the final week.
Tourists arrive already bewildered by a menu that lists forty dumplings by number and nothing else.
Nothing bewilders a new parent faster than three brands of car seat and a manual translated from German by a machine.
words.etymology: be-(使) + wilder(迷失荒野) → 使人如入荒野般困惑

meanings.en: to be a sign or warning that something, usually something bad, is going to happen
meanings.zh: 预示,预兆(多指不祥之事)

examples: Analysts argued that three straight quarters of falling orders portend a hiring freeze long before any memo reaches the staff.
The cracked tile in the ceiling portended a leak that arrived, right on schedule, during the first heavy rain of October.
In the film, every crow on the fence portends something, which makes the ninety minutes feel longer than they are.
A goalkeeper limping off in the eleventh minute rarely portends a comfortable afternoon for the two thousand fans who traveled.
Nothing about the calm Tuesday morning portended the outage that would take the payment system down for eleven hours.
words.etymology: por-(向前) + tendere(伸展) → 预先伸出征兆

meanings.en: to talk or write at length in a confused, aimless way that is hard to follow
meanings.zh: 漫无边际地说,东拉西扯

meanings.en: to walk for pleasure, especially in the countryside, without following a fixed route
a long, unhurried walk taken for pleasure

examples: The keynote speaker rambled for twenty minutes about his first startup before anyone realized he had skipped the actual product demo.
My uncle rambles through three unrelated stories every Thanksgiving and somehow lands, at the end, exactly on the point he wanted.
The review rambles for six paragraphs about parking before mentioning that the restaurant's noodles were, in fact, excellent.
Retirees from the village ramble across the moor every Wednesday, rain or not, and finish at a pub that opens early for them.
A two-hour ramble through the hills left her phone dead, her boots soaked, and her mood better than it had been all week.

meanings.en: trying to appear more important, talented, or cultured than you really are
meanings.zh: 自命不凡的,炫耀的(装出高人一等的样子)

examples: The café charges eleven dollars for toast and calls it a tasting experience, which my sister says is the most pretentious thing in the neighborhood.
His email signature listed four languages he had studied for one semester each, and everyone in the office found it quietly pretentious.
The film runs three hours without dialogue, and even critics who admired it admitted the ending was pretentious rather than profound.
She renamed the shared spreadsheet 'The Ledger of Intentions', which struck the whole team as pretentious for a list of grocery runs.
The wine bar's menu describes a cheap red as 'brooding and architectural', which is pretentious enough to make regulars order beer instead.
words.etymology: prae-(在前) + tendere(伸展) → 在人前摆出姿态

meanings.en: excessively eager to please or obey someone powerful, in a way that seems insincere
meanings.zh: 谄媚的,奉承的(对权势者过分讨好)

examples: The waiter became obsequious the moment he recognized the food critic, refilling water glasses that nobody had touched in twenty minutes.
Her replies to the vice president were so obsequious that colleagues started forwarding them around as a joke.
The chatbot apologizes four times per answer, an obsequious habit that makes users trust its actual corrections less.
He nodded obsequiously through the landlord's entire speech and then complained about the broken heater only in the group chat.
Investors were unnerved by the board's obsequious questions, which sounded rehearsed and never once challenged the founder's revenue forecast.
words.etymology: ob-(朝向) + sequi(跟随) → 一味跟随讨好

meanings.en: making a loud confused noise, or demanding something loudly and persistently
meanings.zh: 喧闹的,吵嚷的(大声而不停地要求)

examples: The stadium was clamorous forty minutes before kickoff, with drums, air horns, and a brass band competing near the south gate.
Parents grew clamorous at the school board meeting once the superintendent admitted the new bus routes were already finalized.
A clamorous flock of crows took over the parking lot every evening, and nobody in the office could hold a phone call outside.
The comments section turned clamorous within an hour, demanding refunds in six languages before the studio had posted any statement.
Rain on the tin roof was so clamorous that the interviewer gave up and rescheduled the recording for the following morning.
words.etymology: clamare(呼喊) + -ous → 喧嚷不休的

meanings.en: the act of making a fault or offence seem less serious by giving reasons for it, or a reason offered for this purpose
meanings.zh: 减轻罪责,辩解(为过失开脱的理由)

examples: The lawyer offered his client's sleepless double shift in extenuation, but the judge kept the full fine in place.
In extenuation of his late rent, the tenant produced three months of hospital receipts and a letter from his employer.
She apologized for the missed deadline without extenuation, which surprised a manager used to hearing about traffic and broken laptops.
The airline's statement mixed apology with extenuation, blaming a vendor's software update for stranding passengers across three time zones.
Reviewers accepted the restaurant's extenuation about the flooded kitchen, but three of them still dropped it a full star.
words.etymology: ex-(向外) + tenuis(薄的) → 把过错说轻,减罪

meanings.en: the quality of not talking much about your own abilities or achievements
behavior or clothing intended to avoid attracting attention or causing offence
meanings.zh: 端庄,得体(着装或举止上)

examples: She accepted the engineering prize with real modesty, thanking the two interns whose failed prototype had taught the team the most.
His modesty about the marathon time was undermined by the finish photo he set as his profile picture that same night.
False modesty is its own kind of bragging, as anyone who has read a startup founder's resignation post can confirm.
The chef's modesty vanished the moment someone mentioned his sourdough, which he described for eleven minutes without pausing for questions.
The dress code asked for modesty in the temple courtyard, so the guide handed out long scarves at the ticket window.
words.etymology: modus(尺度) + -ty → 有分寸,不自夸

meanings.en: a feeling of unhappiness or dissatisfaction, especially with your situation or with people in authority
meanings.zh: 不满,不满情绪(对处境或当权者)

meanings.en: feeling dissatisfied and wanting a situation to change

examples: Rising rents turned quiet discontent into a tenants' union that filled the council chamber on a Tuesday night in February.
The exit survey buried the real discontent under a question about snacks, so leadership read the results as a catering problem.
Fan discontent over the season finale filled forums for weeks, and the showrunner deleted her account before the reunion special aired.
Nurses expressed their discontent by wearing black armbands through three shifts before the hospital agreed to reopen contract talks.
Shareholders remain discontent with a bonus scheme that pays out even in the years the factory misses every delivery target.

meanings.en: shyness and lack of confidence in one's own worth or ability, especially in front of other people

examples: She answered the interviewer's questions with a diffidence that hid three years of shipping code nobody else on the team could read.
His diffidence at the standup meeting vanished the moment someone asked about the database migration he had spent the weekend rewriting.
The pianist walked onstage with such diffidence that the audience assumed a student had wandered up before the real performer arrived.
Years of being interrupted in meetings had bred a diffidence she was now unlearning, one raised hand at a time.
He apologized for his own question with the diffidence of a first-year student, then asked something the professor could not answer.
words.etymology: dis-(不) + fidere(信任) → 不自信

meanings.en: pleasant to listen to, with a smooth and tuneful sound

examples: The subway violinist's melodious cover of a video-game theme stopped a dozen commuters who were already late for work.
Her voice on the podcast is so melodious that listeners keep the episode playing long after they have stopped following the argument.
The doorbell plays a melodious three-note chime that the previous owner recorded himself, and nobody in the family can change it.
Blackbirds sing melodiously outside the hospital window at four in the morning, indifferent to the patients trying to sleep through it.
The error message on the new washing machine arrives as a melodious little tune rather than the harsh beep everyone expects.
words.etymology: melos(曲调) + ōidē(歌唱) → 曲调悦耳的

meanings.en: famous and highly respected within a particular profession or field of knowledge
meanings.zh: 杰出的,著名的(指某领域的权威)

examples: The conference flew in an eminent climate scientist who spent most of her keynote explaining why the previous speaker's chart was misleading.
Three eminent surgeons signed the letter, and the hospital board reversed the staffing decision within a week of it appearing online.
My grandfather kept a photograph of himself shaking hands with an eminent judge who later turned out to be taking bribes.
The obituary described him as an eminent translator, though he had spent his last decade writing crossword puzzles for a local paper.
Her lab is far too small for someone this eminent, but she refuses to move until the university replaces the ventilation.
words.etymology: e-(向外) + minere(凸起) → 高出众人的

meanings.en: the state of being important, well known, or easy to notice
a part that sticks out or rises above what surrounds it, such as a rocky height
meanings.zh: 突出物,凸起处(如高地、日珥)

examples: The bassist rose to prominence after a thirty-second clip of her warm-up routine circulated on TikTok during the strike.
The redesign gives the unsubscribe link the same prominence as the buy button, which the marketing team fought against for months.
Climate adaptation gained prominence in the budget debate only after two floods closed the same highway in a single spring.
Her name appears on the poster with a prominence that annoys the three co-authors listed below in six-point grey type.
The trail ends at a rocky prominence where hikers queue for twenty minutes to photograph the valley from exactly the same spot.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + minere(凸起) → 凸出,引人注目

meanings.en: extremely ugly or unpleasant to look at, to the point of being shocking

examples: The landlord painted the entire flat a hideous shade of mustard and raised the rent two hundred pounds for the refurbishment.
My aunt knits a hideous Christmas sweater for me every year, and I have worn each one exactly once, in photographs.
The concert hall is acoustically perfect and hideous from the outside, a concrete block the city has tried three times to demolish.
Traffic was hideously slow on the bridge, so the ambulance crew took the tunnel and reached the hospital eleven minutes faster.
The mask he wore to the school play was so hideous that two children in the front row started crying immediately.

meanings.en: too ready to believe what others say, and therefore easy to trick or cheat

examples: The scam targets gullible investors with screenshots of returns that any spreadsheet could produce in about four minutes.
I am gullible enough to believe every delivery text I receive, which is why my sister now manages my parcels.
He assumed his grandmother was gullible about technology, then watched her spot a phishing email he had already clicked twice.
New students are the most gullible market on campus, which is why three credit-card stalls appear outside the library every September.
The prank works only on someone gullible enough to hold a phone to their ear and repeat whatever the caller says.

meanings.en: the single most important point of a problem or argument, the one that decides everything else
meanings.zh: 关键,症结,最核心的难点

examples: The crux of the housing dispute is not the rent itself but who pays to replace the leaking roof.
Her lawyer skipped the timeline and went straight to the crux: nobody could produce the signed delivery receipt.
The crux of the interview came when they asked why she had left her previous job after eleven weeks.
Every review of the electric hatchback circles the same crux: charging time, not price, decides whether commuters switch.
We argued about fonts for an hour before someone named the crux, which was that the deadline had already slipped.
words.etymology: crux(十字,交叉) → 各方交汇处,即问题的关键

meanings.en: based on the mathematics of chance, giving likelihoods rather than one certain answer

examples: The weather app switched to a probabilistic forecast, so instead of rain at three it now shows a sixty percent chance.
Her thesis replaces the rigid rules engine with a probabilistic model that learns which loan applications a human would flag.
Chess engines now judge positions with a probabilistic score, offering a win percentage instead of the confident evaluations of the nineties.
Doctors gave a probabilistic answer about the surgery, which frustrated my father, who wanted a yes or a no.
Insurance pricing is probabilistic at heart: the company never knows your crash risk, only what drivers like you did.

meanings.en: a statement or idea that you take as true and build an argument, plan, or story on
meanings.zh: 前提,假定(论证或计划的出发点)

meanings.en: the building and land that a company or organization occupies, normally used in the plural form premises
meanings.zh: 经营场所,房屋及地产(常用复数premises)

examples: The whole startup rests on the premise that people will pay monthly for software they used to buy once.
Half the show's jokes collapse because its premise, that nobody in the office owns a smartphone, stopped being believable.
The budget was built on a false premise: that fuel prices would stay flat through a war and an election.
Staff were told to leave the premises by six so the landlord could change every lock over the weekend.
The cafe lost its license after inspectors found two freezers on the premises running eight degrees too warm.

relatedForms.zh: (企业的)房屋与土地,经营场所

words.etymology: prae-(在前) + mittere(送出,放置) → 先行摆出的前提

meanings.en: seeming reasonable or likely to be true, although it has not been proved
meanings.zh: 貌似有理的,看似可信的

examples: His excuse about the train sounded plausible until we saw the photo of him at brunch that morning.
The only plausible explanation for the missing files is that the intern cleaned the shared drive before leaving.
Deepfake voices are now plausible enough that our finance team verifies every transfer request with a call back.
Every alibi in the podcast is plausible on its own, but three of them cannot all be true at once.
The startup's revenue projection looked plausible on the slide until an investor asked how many salespeople it assumed.
words.etymology: plaudere(鼓掌) + -ible(可…的) → 值得鼓掌的,即看似可信

meanings.en: an offer or plan put to someone, or a thing judged by how difficult or worthwhile it would be
meanings.zh: 提议,交易方案,(需要权衡的)一件事

meanings.en: a statement that puts forward an idea and can be judged true or false
meanings.zh: 命题,论断(可判断真假的陈述)

examples: He pitched it as a simple proposition: we host the site free, and they let us keep the analytics.
Opening a bookshop next to a university sounds romantic, but as a business proposition it depends entirely on the rent.
Driving eleven hours to save ninety dollars on a mattress is a losing proposition once you count fuel and hotels.
The seminar spent an hour on a single proposition: that a machine can be wrong without ever being dishonest.
Each proposition in the report is footnoted, so a reader can check whether the claim about wages survives the data.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + ponere(放置) → 摆到前面的提议或命题

meanings.en: the quality of seeming reasonable or believable, whether or not it is actually true
meanings.zh: 貌似合理，可信度（似真而未必真）

examples: The alibi had a surface plausibility that collapsed once detectives pulled the parking garage footage from that Tuesday night.
Reviewer two questioned the plausibility of the model's assumption that every user reads the privacy notice before clicking accept.
The screenwriter added a rain-soaked bus stop to the scene purely to lend plausibility to the couple's improbable second meeting.
Investors weighed the plausibility of the startup's claim that it could cut delivery times in half using bicycles alone.
The report's plausibility rests on one assumption: that nobody in the warehouse ever signed for a delivery they had not counted.
words.etymology: plaudere(鼓掌) → 值得喝彩的 → 说得通的

meanings.en: believable; convincing enough to be accepted as true
meanings.zh: 可信的，可靠的（说法、证据、证人）

meanings.en: good enough to be taken seriously as a real possibility or contender
meanings.zh: 有实力的，像样的（候选人、对手、威胁）

examples: The witness sounded credible until the defense produced a timestamped receipt placing her forty miles from the intersection that evening.
Editors spiked the story because its single source was an anonymous Telegram account with no credible evidence beyond a blurry screenshot.
Three weeks before the primary, the mayor was still the only credible challenger with money and a ground operation.
Security treated the emailed threat as credible after the sender listed the building's badge reader locations correctly.
The consultant argued credibly that switching warehouses would cut shipping costs, then produced six months of freight invoices.
words.etymology: credere(相信) → 可以相信的 → 可信的

meanings.en: to suppose that something is true without proof, on the basis of what seems likely
meanings.zh: 推定，假定（无确证而认定如此）

meanings.en: to be bold enough to do something one has no right or standing to do; to take unfair advantage of someone's goodwill
meanings.zh: 冒昧，擅自（做无权做的事）；不知分寸地利用

examples: Rescuers presumed the hikers had taken the ridge trail, since their car was still parked at the eastern trailhead.
The court presumes every defendant innocent, which is why the prosecutor spent nine days building the timeline.
I presume the invoice already went out, but check with accounting before you tell the client anything.
I would not presume to rewrite a surgeon's checklist after one week of shadowing her in the operating room.
The new hire presumed on his manager's patience, forwarding vacation photos to a client thread twice in one week.
words.etymology: prae-(先) + sumere(拿取) → 先取为定 → 推定

meanings.en: capable of being legally transferred to another person or party
meanings.zh: 可转让的，可让与的（合同、权利、票据）

meanings.en: able to be attributed to a specific cause, person, or category
meanings.zh: 可归因的，可归属的（原因、责任）

examples: The lease is assignable only with the landlord's written consent, which she withheld until the new tenant produced two pay stubs.
Startup lawyers flagged the clause: the license was not assignable, so the acquisition would have voided their biggest customer contract.
None of the defects were assignable to a single supplier, so the plant audited all four before restarting the line.
The delay had no assignable cause in the logs, just eleven minutes of silence between the last heartbeat and the alarm.
Season tickets became assignable this year, and half the section quietly sold their playoff seats to a resale site.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + signare(标记) → 标定归属 → 可转让的

meanings.en: in spite of; despite — placed either before or after the noun it governs
meanings.zh: 尽管，虽有（可前置，亦可后置于所修饰的名词）

meanings.en: all the same; nevertheless
meanings.zh: 尽管如此，仍然（多置于句末）

meanings.en: although; despite the fact that — usually introducing a clause with that
meanings.zh: 虽然，尽管（引导从句，常作 notwithstanding that）

examples: The store opened on schedule notwithstanding the shipping delay, its shelves half stocked with cartons borrowed from a rival warehouse.
The rain notwithstanding, four hundred people stood outside the courthouse until the verdict was read at nine.
The hospital rolled out the scheduling app to every ward in March, notwithstanding two failed pilots and a nurses' petition.
Her landlord had raised the rent twice in a year; she renewed the lease notwithstanding, because the commute was fifteen minutes.
The vendor kept shipping parts for another six weeks, notwithstanding that the contract had expired the previous December.
words.etymology: not + withstanding(抵挡) → 不为其所阻 → 尽管

meanings.en: pleased with yourself and your situation, and so no longer alert to risks or shortcomings
meanings.zh: 自满的，自鸣得意的（因满足现状而放松警惕）

examples: Two quarters of record sales made the team complacent, and nobody noticed the churn rate climbing until January.
The champions played complacently in the first half and were two goals down before the coach started shouting.
Auditors warn that a decade without a breach makes security teams complacent about rotating the keys nobody remembers issuing.
She refused to grow complacent after the promotion and spent Saturday mornings learning the query language her analysts used.
The town became complacent about the levee, mowing its grass every spring but never funding the inspection engineers requested.
words.etymology: com-(全然) + placere(使愉悦) → 自我满足 → 自满的

meanings.en: a feeling that something has fallen short of what one wanted or expected
meanings.zh: 不满，不满意（对待遇、服务、现状）

examples: Exit interviews traced most of the dissatisfaction to the new on-call rota, which put junior engineers on call three weekends a month.
Her dissatisfaction with the flat showed within a week: the boiler groaned all night and the landlord stopped answering.
The survey buried customer dissatisfaction under a 4.2-star average, but the written comments all named the same 40-minute checkout queue.
Two years of quiet dissatisfaction ended when he handed in his notice and took a pay cut to teach secondary-school physics.
Fans voiced their dissatisfaction with the ending in a 300-page thread, and the studio quietly commissioned a re-edit.
words.etymology: dis-(否定) + satis(足够) + facere(做) → 未做到足够 → 不满

meanings.en: restlessly unhappy with one's situation and inclined to show it
meanings.zh: 心怀不满的，不满足的（对处境、待遇）

examples: A discontented night shift is why the warehouse lost a third of its pickers before the holiday rush even started.
She grew discontented in the role six months in, once she realized nobody read the reports she spent every Thursday writing.
The discontented shareholders filed a motion to replace two board members after the third straight quarter of missed targets.
He scrolled discontentedly through job listings on the train home, comparing each salary band with the raise his manager promised in March.
Fifteen years in the same open-plan office had left him discontented but too close to his pension to walk out.
words.etymology: dis-(否定) + contentus(满足的) → 不满足的

meanings.en: drained of enthusiasm and hope, usually after a setback
meanings.zh: 沮丧的，气馁的（受挫后失去干劲）

examples: The team came off the pitch dispirited after conceding twice in stoppage time to a side sitting bottom of the table.
Three rounds of rejections left her dispirited enough to close the laptop and take a week off from applying.
A dispirited crowd of forty sat through the second act, and the producers announced the closing date the next morning.
He typed the same status update for the fourth week running, dispirited by a project nobody upstream seemed to be reading.
The volunteers packed up the leftover flyers dispiritedly, having registered nine voters in six hours outside the supermarket.
words.etymology: dis-(去除) + spiritus(气息、精神) → 失去精神 → 沮丧

meanings.en: the state of having become distant or hostile toward someone once close
meanings.zh: 疏远，隔阂；断绝往来（多指亲人、伴侣之间）

examples: Their estrangement lasted eleven years and ended in a hospital corridor, when neither could remember what the original argument was about.
The will mentioned his estrangement from the family in a single line, then left the farmhouse to a cousin.
Years of missed birthdays hardened into estrangement, and she stopped explaining to colleagues why her mother never called.
The therapist described the estrangement between the brothers as the cheapest solution either had found to a decade of arguing about money.
A single text about the wedding guest list triggered an estrangement that survived two Christmases and one shared funeral.
words.etymology: ex-(向外) + extraneus(外来的) → 变成外人 → 疏远

meanings.en: the feeling of being accepted as a member of a group or place
meanings.zh: 归属感（被群体或某地接纳的感觉）

meanings.en: (plural) the personal possessions a person owns and carries

examples: The Sunday football league gave him a sense of belonging that eighteen months of after-work drinks never managed to.
Universities keep surveying first-year students about their sense of belonging, then cut the very societies where the shy ones found it.
After twenty years abroad, he felt no belonging in either country, and said so at his father's funeral.
She packed her belongings into two suitcases and a bike pannier, and left the flat keys on the kitchen counter.
Airport staff photograph every unclaimed bag, and belongings nobody collects within ninety days are auctioned off in bulk.

meanings.en: to slip back into a bad habit or worse condition after making progress
meanings.zh: 故态复萌，倒退（戒除或改善后又退回原状）

examples: Two weeks after quitting, he began to backslide, buying one pack at the petrol station and calling it a weekend exception.
Teams that hold a code-review standard for two quarters still backslide the moment a release date moves up.
The clinic tracks how many patients backslide within a year, and publishes the number whether or not it flatters them.
Observers warned that the country was backsliding when the election commission lost its power to certify the results.
She reads her old journal whenever she feels herself backsliding, and the entry from January usually gets her back to the pool.

meanings.en: well known and important; standing out among others of the same kind
meanings.zh: 著名的，重要的（人物、机构、角色）

meanings.en: easily seen or noticed; sticking out from a surface
meanings.zh: 显眼的，突出的（位置、特征）

examples: She became a prominent voice in the housing debate after a single thread about her rent increase reached two million readers.
The bakery earned a prominent mention in the city's food guide, and the Saturday queue now wraps past the laundromat.
The recall notice sat at the bottom of the page in grey type, nowhere near as prominent as the discount banner above it.
The scar across his knuckle is prominent enough that clients notice it during handshakes, and he has stopped explaining where it came from.
The pitch deck gave the single enterprise customer a prominent slot on every slide, while eleven smaller logos crowded the footer.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + minere(突出) → 向前凸出 → 显著的

meanings.en: in a way that is easily seen or noticed, or that gives something importance
meanings.zh: 显著地，醒目地（陈列、提及、出现）

examples: The museum hung the disputed painting prominently at the entrance, with a placard admitting the attribution is still argued over.
Her name appears prominently on the patent, though she left the company two years before the filing went through.
The allergy warning is printed prominently on the front of the box, in red, right above the barcode.
Sponsor logos featured prominently in the highlight reel, occupying more screen time than the winning goal itself.
The unsubscribe link sits at the bottom in six-point grey, while the upgrade button sits prominently under the first paragraph.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + minere(突出) → 向前凸出 → 显著地

meanings.en: the highest or final point of something that has developed over a long time
meanings.zh: 顶点，高潮；（长期努力的）最终结果

examples: The exhibition is the culmination of six years spent photographing the same stretch of coastline every February.
Winning the district contract was the culmination of a campaign that started with one parent counting potholes on her commute.
The merger announcement was less a surprise than the culmination of eighteen months of quiet hiring from the same three firms.
Her keynote felt like the culmination of a decade of unread blog posts, finally delivered to a room of fifteen hundred.
The strike was the culmination of two years of missed raises, not the impulsive walkout the press release described.
collocations: the culmination of years of effort
words.etymology: culmen(山顶) + -ation → 登上顶峰 → 顶点，高潮

meanings.en: confusing and hard to explain, because the facts do not fit together
meanings.zh: 令人费解的，令人困惑的（问题、行为、数据）

examples: The bug is perplexing: it appears only on Tuesdays, only for users in one time zone, and never in staging.
She found his silence perplexing, since he had spent the whole week asking to be put on the project.
The most perplexing part of the survey was that satisfaction rose in every branch while overall satisfaction fell.
Assembly instructions with fourteen unlabeled screws and one perplexing diagram cost him an entire Saturday and most of his patience.
Doctors called the scan perplexing, because the fracture had healed cleanly, yet the pain had moved to the other ankle.
words.etymology: per-(彻底) + plexus(缠绕) → 完全缠住 → 令人困惑

meanings.en: a junction where two or more highways meet, connected by ramps
meanings.zh: 互通式立交，高速公路交叉口

meanings.en: an exchange of ideas, information, or people between two sides
meanings.zh: 交流，互换（思想、信息、人员）

meanings.en: to exchange two things so that each takes the other's place

examples: Traffic backed up two miles at the interchange after a jackknifed truck closed the ramp onto the northbound freeway.
The city spent four years rebuilding the interchange, and drivers now save eleven minutes on the morning commute.
The workshop was worth the flight less for the talks than for the interchange between clinicians and the engineers building their software.
A brief interchange in the hallway settled a dispute that three weeks of email threads had only made worse.
Editors interchanged the two chapter titles by mistake, and the error survived three proof rounds before a reader flagged it.
words.etymology: inter-(相互) + change(交换) → 互相交换；交叉口

meanings.en: able to be used in place of each other without making any difference
meanings.zh: 可互换的，可替代的（零件、术语、人员）

examples: The two batteries look identical but are not interchangeable, and using the wrong one voids the drone's warranty.
Journalists use the two terms interchangeably, though economists insist one measures income and the other measures wealth.
Treating the night nurses as interchangeable cost the ward its best-performing team within a single quarter.
The furniture line sells on one promise: every shelf, leg, and bracket is interchangeable across all nine models.
Reviewers complained the three lead characters were interchangeable, differing only in hair color and which coffee they ordered.
words.etymology: inter-(相互) + change(交换) + -able(可…的) → 可互换的

meanings.en: easily annoyed or made angry, especially as a standing trait of temperament
meanings.zh: 易怒的，动辄发火的（指脾气秉性，一点小事就上火）

examples: Three hours into the delayed layover, even the calmest people at the gate had turned irritable and were snapping at the airline staff.
My father grows irritable whenever the Wi-Fi drops mid-broadcast, muttering at the router as though it can hear him.
Two weeks of night shifts left her permanently irritable; she apologized to her roommate twice a day for a tone she could not control.
The new manager is brilliant but irritable, and the team has learned to bring him problems only after his second coffee.
Her irritable replies in the code review thread had nothing to do with the pull request and everything to do with a broken sleep schedule.
words.etymology: irritare(激怒) + -able(易…的) → 易怒的

meanings.en: bad-tempered and quick to complain, especially because of tiredness, hunger, or discomfort (informal)
meanings.zh: 脾气暴躁的，闹别扭的（口语；多因困倦、饥饿或不适而一时如此）

examples: The toddler got cranky at the museum around four o'clock, and no amount of dinosaur skeletons could distract him from the missed nap.
I get cranky if I skip lunch, so my team schedules the hard conversations for eleven and never for four.
Everyone was cranky by the third hour of the road trip, three of them hungry and nobody willing to stop again.
She warned her roommate she would be cranky until the espresso machine finished heating, and asked for ten quiet minutes.
The whole newsroom turned cranky during the election-night shift, surviving on cold pizza and refreshing the county results every ninety seconds.

meanings.en: willing to accept control or instruction without resisting; easily managed
meanings.zh: 温顺的，唯命是从的（顺从到不加反抗的地步）

examples: The board expected a docile chief executive and got one who cancelled the merger in his first week.
Years of layoffs had left the staff docile: nobody questioned the new attendance policy, though everyone complained in the parking lot.
The regime prefers a docile press, so editors learn which stories die quietly before they ever reach a copy desk.
Teachers who reward docile students end up punishing the ones who ask why, and the classroom gets quieter every year.
The shelter described the dog as docile, and he slept through the entire drive home without once lifting his head.
words.etymology: docere(教) + -ile(易…的) → 易受教的 → 温顺的

meanings.en: enduring pain or hardship without showing feeling or complaining
meanings.zh: 隐忍的，坚忍克己的（默默承受痛苦而不诉苦）

meanings.en: a person who endures hardship without complaint or visible emotion
meanings.zh: 隐忍克己的人，能默默扛住苦难的人

examples: He stayed stoic through the whole chemotherapy schedule, joking about the parking rates while his wife did the crying for both of them.
The goalkeeper was stoic about the penalty that ended the season, answering every reporter's question without once blaming the referee.
My grandmother kept a stoic silence about the eviction for three weeks, and we only learned of it from a neighbor.
Nurses on the night shift are stoics by necessity; they finish a twelve-hour rotation and then ask whether anyone needs a hand.
Everyone expected tears when the verdict was read, but the defendant remained stoic and thanked her lawyer in a level voice.
words.etymology: stoa(希腊柱廊) → 柱廊下讲学的学派 → 隐忍克己

meanings.en: showing no feeling or reaction in the face; blank
meanings.zh: 面无表情的（脸上看不出任何情绪）

examples: The border officer stayed expressionless while I explained the missing stamp, then slid my passport back without a word.
Her expressionless face on the video call made the layoff announcement harder; nobody could tell whether she agreed with it.
The poker champion sat expressionless behind tinted glasses for six hours, giving the table nothing to read.
Botox left the actor expressionless in close-ups, and the director cut every reaction shot from the third act.
The teenager kept an expressionless face through the whole lecture about curfew, then asked whether he could still borrow the car.

meanings.en: continuing without pause or any reduction in intensity
meanings.zh: 持续不断的，丝毫不减弱的（雨、压力、批评等）

meanings.en: refusing to give up or to show mercy in pursuing something
meanings.zh: 不屈不挠的；毫不留情的（指人穷追不舍）

examples: The rain was relentless for nine days, and the sandbags at the front door stopped mattering by Thursday.
Under relentless pressure from investors, the founder cut a third of the staff and still missed the quarterly target.
She is relentless about deadlines: three reminders before noon, and a calendar invite for the reminder about the reminder.
The prosecutor was relentless in cross-examination, returning to the same four minutes of security footage until the witness changed his story.
The team's relentless press wore the visitors down; by the seventieth minute their defenders were walking back to position.
words.etymology: lentus(柔软) → relent(心软) + -less → 毫不松懈

meanings.en: happening earlier than the proper or expected time, especially of a death or ending
meanings.zh: 过早的，早于应有时间的（去世、结束、凋零）

meanings.en: coming at a moment when it is unwelcome or badly timed
meanings.zh: 来得不是时候的（打断、伤病、消息）

examples: The band's reunion tour was cancelled after the drummer's untimely death at forty-one, three weeks before the first show in Detroit.
Her grandmother's untimely stroke at fifty-two pushed the whole family into a conversation about wills that nobody wanted to have.
The fire alarm went off during the CEO's closing pitch, an untimely interruption that cost the startup its only shot at the round.
Frost in early May brought an untimely end to the orchard's blossom, and the co-op cut its apple forecast by half.
The striker's untimely injury in the eighty-ninth minute left the team with ten men and no substitutions remaining.

meanings.en: occurring at an awkward or unwelcome moment, so that it causes difficulty or embarrassment
meanings.zh: 时机不巧的，令人为难的（造访、提问、请求）

examples: The video call froze at an inopportune moment, leaving my face mid-sneeze on thirty screens for the rest of the quarterly review.
My landlord chose an inopportune time to raise the rent, the same week my contract ended and my savings hit zero.
The toddler asked how babies are made at an inopportune moment, halfway through dinner with my wife's very traditional parents.
The storm arrived at the most inopportune hour of the day, ten minutes before an outdoor wedding that had taken a year to plan.
Asking for a raise the morning after the department missed its targets was inopportune, and my manager's face said so before she did.
words.etymology: in-(不) + ob-(朝) + portus(港口) → 顺风入港 → 不合时宜

meanings.en: a shortage of something needed, where the available supply falls short of demand
meanings.zh: 短缺，稀缺（资源、劳动力、供给；经济学术语）

examples: Chip scarcity kept the dealership's lot half empty for eight months, and the used Corolla out front sold for more than a new one.
Water scarcity in the valley has pushed almond growers to drip irrigation and, in three districts, to fallowing a quarter of their fields.
The sneaker brand manufactures scarcity on purpose, releasing four hundred pairs a month so resale prices stay triple the retail sticker.
Economics students spend the first lecture on scarcity: unlimited wants, limited resources, and every choice therefore costing something else.
A scarcity of qualified electricians has stalled the city's heat-pump rollout, with homeowners now waiting five months for an installation date.

meanings.en: a serious lack of something, especially of something abstract such as evidence, talent, or ideas
meanings.zh: 匮乏，奇缺（证据、人才、想象力等抽象事物；书面语）

examples: The inquiry collapsed for a dearth of evidence: two witnesses recanted and the only email chain had been deleted in a routine purge.
After four rounds of interviews the panel reported a dearth of candidates who could actually write, only ones who could talk about writing.
For all its budget, the sequel suffers from a dearth of imagination: three chase scenes, and every one of them borrowed.
A dearth of trust between the two departments turned a one-week handover into a four-month negotiation over who owned the data.
The city hall beat is down to one part-timer, and the dearth of local reporting shows in how many contracts pass unread.
words.etymology: dēore(昂贵) + -th(名词后缀) → 物贵而少 → 匮乏

meanings.en: to hold back a feeling, impulse, or memory so that it is not expressed or recalled
meanings.zh: 压抑，克制（情绪、笑意、记忆）

meanings.en: to put down opposition or a group by force or authority
meanings.zh: 镇压，压制（抗议、异议、少数族群）

examples: She repressed a laugh when the CFO called the layoffs a talent reallocation, then bit her pen for the rest of the slide.
Her therapist doubts she repressed the memory so much as rehearsed a softer version of it every year until it replaced the original.
The regime repressed the protests by cutting mobile data for six days and arresting anyone who had posted a map of the marches.
For decades the ministry repressed the region's minority schools, and now elderly speakers are being recorded before the language disappears.
He spent the whole custody hearing repressing his anger, answering in flat sentences while his hands shook under the table.
words.etymology: re-(向后) + premere(压) → 压回去 → 压抑，镇压

meanings.en: causing a strong feeling of disgust or revulsion
meanings.zh: 令人厌恶的，令人反感的（行为、言论、外表）

examples: The comment section under the video was so repulsive that the artist deleted her account and moved her portfolio to a private site.
He found the whole business model repulsive, charging grieving families a subscription to keep a memorial page online, and resigned in March.
The villain's mask tested badly with children, less frightening than repulsive, so the studio reshot four scenes with a plainer design.
Something repulsive was growing in the office fridge, and by Thursday nobody would eat lunch on the fourth floor.
Her ex's habit of reading her texts aloud to friends struck me as repulsive long before she found the courage to leave.
words.etymology: re-(回) + pellere(推) → 把人推开 → 令人排斥

meanings.en: for the same reason, applied to a parallel case; often introducing the other side of a logic you have just accepted
meanings.zh: 同理；照这个道理（承认上一句后，把同一条逻辑用到另一边）

examples: We charge less for domestic flights, but by the same token, our budget for cabin amenities is close to nothing.
If the landlord can raise the rent over a new boiler, then by the same token he owes us heat in November.
You shouldn't ignore a dripping tap; by the same token, a small crack in your windshield needs attention this week.
She never answers email after seven, and by the same token she expects no reply from her team at midnight.
Crypto can double overnight. By the same token, one badly worded tweet can wipe out a portfolio before breakfast.
words.etymology: token(古义:凭据、标记) → 凭同一条依据 → 同理

meanings.en: said before offering information or an opinion that the listener may not need, want, or accept
meanings.zh: 说了也未必有用，但还是提一句（自谦地引出信息或看法）

examples: I know you've finalized the menu, but for what it's worth, three of the wedding guests cannot go near peanuts.
The client hated our pitch deck, though for what it's worth, the marketing director asked for a copy of the last slide.
My mechanic says the transmission is finished. But for what it's worth, the stereo still sounds incredible.
I found a leather jacket in the lost property bin, and for what it's worth, there is a set of keys in the pocket.
The gallery turned my portfolio down last week. For what it's worth, they said the charcoal sketches were worth pursuing.
collocations: for what it's worth, I think

meanings.en: in itself, judged on its own terms rather than by what surrounds it or follows from it
meanings.zh: 本身；就其本身而言（常与否定连用，否认问题出在事物本身）

examples: The sudden resignation of the chief executive was not a crisis per se, but it triggered a sell-off by Thursday.
She doesn't dislike your dog per se; she objects to the muddy paw prints on her silk cushions every Tuesday.
The new zoning rules do not ban rooftop bars per se, but the noise limits are strict enough that nobody builds them.
It was not an interrogation per se, but the border agent kept asking why my passport had no exit stamp from Cairo.
Night shifts are not harmful per se, provided you keep a rigid sleep schedule behind blackout curtains during the day.
words.etymology: 拉丁 per(凭借) + se(自身) → 就其本身而言

meanings.en: to have a strong influence that persists long afterwards, usually an oppressive or unwelcome one
meanings.zh: 影响深远且久久不散（多为负面的笼罩感）

examples: The founder's conviction continues to cast a long shadow over the startup's ability to raise serious money.
A childhood spent in poverty casts a long shadow, altering forever how someone reads the price on a carton of milk.
The collapse of the regional bank is casting a long shadow over every local business that runs on short-term credit.
Her predecessor won three straight championships, casting a long shadow that makes any narrow win look like a failure.
Chernobyl still casts a long shadow across European energy policy, pushing money toward solar and wind instead.

meanings.en: with skepticism; not treating a claim as fully or literally true
meanings.zh: 打个折扣地信，别全当真（多用于 take/treat … with a pinch of salt）

examples: Given that the blog is paid for by a dairy group, take its study on the health benefits of cheese with a pinch of salt.
Whenever the estate agent calls a neighbourhood up and coming, you have to take it with a pinch of salt.
His official biography claims eighteen holes-in-one in a single round, a figure historians treat with a pinch of salt.
I read anonymous reviews with a pinch of salt, since the people most likely to write them were just fired.
You should take her excuses with a pinch of salt; she has now claimed a flat tyre on three separate Mondays.
collocations: take it with a pinch of salt
treat with a pinch of salt
words.etymology: 拉丁 cum grano salis(加一粒盐的解毒方) → 打折扣地信

meanings.en: to originate in something, or be caused by it; the subject is the effect and the object is the root
meanings.zh: 源于；由…而起（主语是结果，宾语是根源）

examples: The squeak in the floorboards stems from a single warped joist just outside the bedroom door.
Her opposition to the highway stemmed from losing her childhood home to a compulsory purchase twenty years ago.
Much of the team's bad quarter seems to stem from the move to an open-plan floor nobody asked for.
Detectives concluded that the warehouse fire stemmed from a frayed extension cord rather than deliberate arson.
We are fixing the lag stemming from last month's database migration by moving the two busiest tables off shared disks.
words.etymology: stem(树干) → 从主干长出来 → 源自

meanings.en: to explain something, or to be the reason it happened
to make up a given amount or proportion of a whole

examples: The suspect could not account for the three hours between leaving the bar and reaching his apartment.
A sudden drop in temperature accounts for the cracks that opened across the concrete foundation overnight.
Nobody at head office could account for how fifty laptops left the building over a single weekend.
Smartphones now account for seventy percent of the traffic to our store in the weeks before Christmas.
Together, rent and utilities account for nearly half of my monthly paycheck, leaving very little for groceries.

meanings.en: to fail to happen after having been arranged or planned

examples: We had packed the moving van, but the house purchase fell through when the survey found water under the roof.
If the merger falls through at the last minute, the chief executive will face a shareholder revolt by Friday.
Her plans to study in Tokyo have fallen through, because the embassy turned down her student visa twice.
The bridge loan never came, so our expansion into the European market fell through two weeks before launch.
The peace talks will fall through if neither side agrees to release its prisoners before the deadline on Friday.

meanings.en: stopping and starting again at irregular intervals rather than continuing steadily

examples: The wifi in the basement office is intermittent, so my video calls freeze every few minutes and clients think I hung up.
Intermittent rain all Saturday ruined the outdoor wedding, forcing guests to shuttle between the marquee and their cars with drinks in hand.
The mechanic could not reproduce the fault, because the warning light on my dashboard is intermittent and never appears inside his garage.
Doctors traced her intermittent chest pain to too much coffee rather than her heart, a relief after three weeks of sleepless worrying.
Power in the village has been intermittent since the storm, so the bakery runs its ovens off a generator between midnight and dawn.
words.etymology: inter-(之间) + mittere(送) → 间歇的

meanings.en: used to introduce a statement that reverses or is the opposite of the one just made

examples: Cheap flights to Rome fill up months ahead in July; conversely, in February you can book a window seat the night before.
Praising the team publicly costs nothing and lifts morale; conversely, one sarcastic line in the group chat can sour a whole quarter.
Our older customers still phone the branch to move money; conversely, nobody under thirty in the survey had ever walked into one.
Adding engineers to a late project usually slows it further; conversely, cutting three features from the list can ship it a month early.
Heavy rain in April fattened the harvest; conversely, the dry spell that followed left the reservoir low enough to expose the old bridge.
words.etymology: com-(一起) + vertere(转) → 反过来说

meanings.en: so offensive to your moral sense or your taste that it fills you with disgust
meanings.zh: 令人厌恶的，令人反感的

examples: The idea of charging refugees for blankets struck the volunteers as morally repugnant, and two of them resigned before the shift ended.
I find the whole industry of fake sympathy cards repugnant, yet the shelf at the supermarket keeps growing every single year.
Her boss's habit of reading employees' private messages was repugnant enough that she photographed the screen and forwarded it to the union.
Most viewers found the show's mockery of grieving parents repugnant, and three advertisers pulled out within forty-eight hours of the broadcast.
He was raised to think debt repugnant, so he paid for the entire kitchen renovation in cash saved over eleven years.
words.etymology: re-(反) + pugnare(战斗) → 令人厌恶的

meanings.en: to reach the highest or final point of a long process, usually ending in a particular result

examples: Three years of weekend rehearsals culminated in a single sold-out night at the town hall, and the choir wept through the encore.
The pay negotiations culminate on Friday, when the two sides either sign the deal or the drivers walk out at midnight.
Months of quiet resentment about the new seating plan culminated in a shouting match at the office Christmas party.
Her research on sleep and shift work will culminate in a book that several hospital managers are already dreading.
The festival culminates with a firework display over the harbour, drawing families who camp along the seawall from early afternoon.
words.etymology: culmen(顶峰) + -ate → 达到顶点，告终

meanings.en: to make someone feel confused and slightly worried because they cannot understand something

examples: What perplexes me is how the parcel reached my neighbour's shed when the tracking page still says it left the depot.
The sudden drop in weekend orders perplexed the whole marketing team, since nothing about the menu or the prices had changed.
Rising sea temperatures off the coast continue to perplex the biologists who have counted the same reef every spring since 1998.
It perplexes my grandmother that anyone would pay monthly for a television channel she can already watch for free through the aerial.
The missing hour on the timesheet perplexed the auditor, who called three times before someone admitted the factory clock ran slow.
words.etymology: per-(彻底) + plexus(缠绕) → 使困惑

meanings.en: feeling confused and unsure what is happening or what you should do next

examples: She stared at the parking ticket with a perplexed frown, since the sign clearly said residents could park there until seven.
The plumber looked genuinely perplexed by the knocking noise in the wall and admitted he had never heard anything quite like it.
Perplexed by the new expenses system, half the department simply stopped claiming for taxis and paid out of their own pockets.
My students were perplexed when the exam asked about a chapter I had promised, twice in writing, would not appear.
He came home to find his flatmates perplexed, standing around a suitcase nobody had ordered and nobody was willing to open.
words.etymology: per-(彻底) + plexus(缠绕) → 困惑不解的

meanings.en: extremely unpleasant, in a way that makes you feel sick or morally offended
meanings.zh: 令人作呕的；令人厌恶的

examples: The office fridge had been unplugged over the long weekend, and the revolting smell drove everyone back into the corridor.
My nephew mixed ketchup, orange juice and cold noodles into one bowl, then dared me to taste the revolting result.
Reviewers called the hotel revolting, posting photos of hair in the sink and a mattress stained by the previous guest.
What I find revolting is not the mistake itself, but the way management blamed the intern in a company-wide email.
The documentary showed revolting conditions in the slaughterhouse, and three of my classmates quietly gave up meat that same week.
words.etymology: re-(向后) + volvere(滚动) → 令人反胃

meanings.en: to drive back an attacking force or an advancing crowd by fighting or resisting
to firmly reject an offer, a request, or someone's romantic approach
meanings.zh: 断然拒绝，回绝（提议或求爱）

examples: The defenders repulsed three separate assaults on the bridge before dawn, then radioed for ammunition that never arrived.
Our security team repulsed a crowd of ticketless fans at the north gate, and the concert started only twenty minutes late.
The bank's engineers repulsed the attack for six hours, but customers still could not log in until Tuesday morning.
She repulsed every attempt her landlord made to renegotiate the lease, forwarding each message straight to the tenants' association.
He kept sending flowers to the front desk, but Maya repulsed him so coldly that the receptionist stopped signing for them.
words.etymology: re-(向后) + pellere(推) → 击退

meanings.en: no longer close to or in contact with a relative or friend, usually after a quarrel
meanings.zh: 断绝往来的，形同陌路的

meanings.en: no longer living with your husband or wife, though not necessarily divorced
meanings.zh: 分居的（但未离婚的配偶）

examples: After the argument over their mother's house, my two uncles stayed estranged for eleven years and missed every family wedding.
The obituary listed an estranged son in Vancouver whom none of the neighbors had ever seen at the house.
She flew home for the surgery and sat beside her estranged father, neither of them mentioning the twelve silent years.
Court records show his estranged wife had already moved to Denver with the children when the company filed for bankruptcy.
They remained legally married but estranged, splitting the mortgage by bank transfer and communicating only through a shared parenting app.
words.etymology: extraneus(外部的) → 变成外人 → 疏远

meanings.en: never having happened or existed before, and therefore without an earlier case to compare with
meanings.zh: 前所未有的，史无前例的

examples: Ticket prices hit an unprecedented four hundred dollars, and fans still emptied the arena's online queue in ninety seconds.
The heat wave brought unprecedented power demand, so the utility cut supply to factories before it touched a single household.
Granting a summer intern access to the payroll database was unprecedented, and the audit team wanted to know who approved it.
The small studio's film took three top awards in one night, an unprecedented sweep for a company founded two years ago.
Doctors described the recovery as unprecedented: the patient walked out of the ward six weeks after surgeons rebuilt his spine.
words.etymology: un-(无) + prae-(先前) + cedere(行走) → 前所未有

meanings.en: impossible to hold back, control, or keep within limits
meanings.zh: 无法抑制的；控制不住的

examples: When the adoption papers finally cleared, her joy was uncontainable and she hugged the case worker in the parking lot.
The fire jumped the highway by noon, and the chief admitted on camera that it was now uncontainable.
Rumors about the layoffs proved uncontainable; by lunchtime the entire third floor had seen a screenshot of the spreadsheet.
The puppy's energy was uncontainable in the small apartment, so we started walking him twice before breakfast.
Halfway through the eulogy his grief became uncontainable, and his brother stepped up to finish reading the last two pages.
words.etymology: un-(不) + con-(共同) + tenere(握住) → 无法抑制

meanings.en: boring because it never changes and offers no variety
meanings.zh: 单调乏味的，千篇一律的

meanings.en: spoken or sounded in one unchanging pitch, so that it is tiring to listen to

examples: Packing identical boxes for nine hours a day was so monotonous that I started memorizing podcast episodes to stay awake.
After a monotonous week of spreadsheets, she booked a night train just to watch different scenery through the window.
The suburb's monotonous rows of beige houses made deliveries hard, and the driver circled twice before finding our number.
Hospital food here is monotonous: boiled chicken, boiled carrots, and the same beige soup at every single lunch.
He read the safety briefing in such a monotonous voice that half the row was asleep before takeoff.
words.etymology: mono-(单一) + tonos(音调) → 单调乏味

meanings.en: ordinary and dull, lacking anything interesting or exciting
belonging to the everyday material world rather than to spiritual or higher concerns

examples: Most of my new job is mundane: resetting passwords, chasing invoices, and reformatting the same spreadsheet every Monday morning.
She quit a mundane office role in Shenzhen to run a diving school, and has never once regretted the pay cut.
The documentary makes even mundane details — a parking receipt, a half-eaten sandwich — feel like clues in a murder case.
Behind the glamorous launch video lies the mundane work of testing every button on four hundred different phone models.
The abbot told visitors to leave mundane concerns at the gate, since the monastery measures time in prayers, not quarterly targets.
words.etymology: mundus(世界) → 尘世的、平凡的

meanings.en: a speech or message that strongly urges someone to do something

examples: The coach's half-time exhortation lasted ninety seconds and sent eleven exhausted players back onto the field like a different team.
Her inbox is full of exhortations to 'circle back' and 'own the outcome', none of which explain who fixes the bug.
The pastor ended with an exhortation to feed the neighbors nobody sees, and forty people signed up to deliver meals.
No amount of managerial exhortation will make people answer emails at midnight if the pay stays exactly the same.
Posters in the stairwell carry cheerful exhortations to take the stairs, while the elevator arrives every twelve seconds anyway.
words.etymology: ex-(向外) + hortari(激励) → 劝诫的话

meanings.en: to break a law or an agreement, especially one protecting someone's creative work
meanings.zh: 侵犯（版权、专利）；违反（法规）

meanings.en: to gradually limit or intrude on someone's rights, freedom, or privacy

examples: The studio claims the fan game infringes its copyright, and has given the two students fourteen days to take it down.
Any restaurant that copies our sauce recipe and our logo infringes the trademark, our lawyer said before sending forty letters.
A karaoke bar in Chengdu was fined because its playlist infringed music licenses the owner had never bothered to buy.
Reading employees' private messages to measure productivity clearly infringes on their privacy, whatever the handbook says about company devices.
Residents argue that the new curfew infringes on their right to walk home safely after a late night shift.
words.etymology: in-(向内) + frangere(打破) → 侵犯、违反

meanings.en: needing a lot of time, effort, and patience to finish
(of writing or speech) heavy and awkward, showing the effort that went into it

examples: Sorting twelve years of receipts into folders is laborious, but the accountant refuses to touch the shoebox until it is done.
Restoring the mural was laborious: two conservators spent nine months lifting soot off with cotton swabs the size of matchsticks.
Before the script existed, checking each order by hand was a laborious ritual that ate the whole of every Friday.
Learning to write Chinese characters felt laborious for months, until my hand finally stopped fighting the stroke order.
The novel's opening chapter is so laborious that most readers give up long before the body is even found.
words.etymology: labor(劳苦) + -ous(充满…的) → 费力的

meanings.en: to speak or recite something loudly and dramatically, as if performing to an audience
to speak out passionately against something you disapprove of

examples: He climbed onto a crate outside the station and declaimed his poem to commuters who mostly kept walking.
The drama teacher makes every student declaim four lines of Shakespeare from the back row until the front row hears them.
At the wedding my uncle declaimed a twenty-minute toast in the voice of a nineteenth-century preacher, and the soup went cold.
Tour guides now declaim the founding myth through headsets, so forty tourists hear the same thunderous speech in total silence.
The columnist declaims against smartphones every week, then posts each column to three social networks before lunch.
words.etymology: de-(加强) + clamare(呼喊) → 高声演说

meanings.en: of a very high quality, as food or drink prepared for people with refined taste
a person who knows a great deal about fine food and drink and enjoys them

examples: The gas station now sells gourmet doughnuts at four dollars each, filled with salted caramel and dusted with gold flakes.
The airline promises a gourmet menu in business class, though the pasta still arrives in a foil tray at thirty thousand feet.
She turned her kitchen into a gourmet cat-food business after her tabby refused everything sold in the supermarket.
My father is a gourmet who can name the region of an olive oil, yet he happily eats instant noodles on Sundays.
The restaurant seats twelve, and the gourmets who fly in for it book their tables eleven months ahead.
words.etymology: 法语 gourmet(品酒侍者) → 美食家

meanings.en: annoyingly eager to give orders or to offer help that nobody asked for, especially over small matters
meanings.zh: 好管闲事的;爱指手画脚的

examples: The officious security guard made me sign three separate forms before he would let me carry a birthday cake into my own office.
An officious neighbor measured our hedge with a tape and posted the photos in the building group chat that same evening.
Our team lead is so officious about formatting that he rewrites every slide deck at midnight and emails the changes at dawn.
A waiter hovered by our table all evening, officious to the point of refilling water glasses that nobody had even touched.
The clerk at the passport office turned officious the moment she noticed my form lacked a middle initial, and sent me home.

relatedForms.zh: 多管闲事地;爱摆架子地

words.etymology: officium(职责,效劳) → 过分热心帮忙 → 多管闲事

meanings.en: dangerous in a way that is not obvious, because the risk is hidden or the conditions can change suddenly
meanings.zh: (路面、天气等)暗藏危险的;凶险的

meanings.en: willing to betray someone who trusts you, or involving such a betrayal

examples: Black ice made the mountain pass treacherous, and the delivery van slid into a ditch two miles from the depot.
The trail looks gentle from the parking lot, but loose scree makes the final ridge treacherous once the fog rolls in.
Divers avoid that wreck in August, when treacherous currents pull even strong swimmers under before the boat can reach them.
His treacherous business partner copied the client list, registered a rival company, and sent the pitch deck out the same week.
Only a treacherous friend would forward those private messages to a reporter after ten years of shared holidays and borrowed money.
words.etymology: trichier(欺骗) → 背信弃义 → 暗藏危险

meanings.en: behaving dishonestly, especially by telling lies or hiding the truth in order to get something

examples: The listing was deceitful: the photos hid the mold behind the washing machine, which we only found after signing the lease.
Her ex kept a deceitful second calendar on his phone so the weekend trips would look like client visits to accounting.
Investors called the founder deceitful after learning the demo video had been filmed with actors and a product that did not exist.
It felt deceitful to praise his cooking all evening and then order noodles on the way home, but nobody wanted an argument.
The subscription page uses deceitful wording, hiding the annual charge in gray text under a bright button that says try free.
words.etymology: de-(离开) + capere(抓取) → decipere(诱人上钩) → 欺骗

meanings.en: letting light pass through, but not clear enough to see objects on the other side distinctly
meanings.zh: 半透明的(透光但看不清)

examples: The bathroom door has a translucent panel, so you can see a shape moving behind it but never who is actually inside.
She printed the logo on translucent paper and laid it over the photograph to check how the two layers lined up.
Fresh squid is almost translucent, and the chef sends back any box where the flesh has already turned chalky and white.
Simmer the onions until they go soft and translucent, then add the garlic so that it does not burn in the pan.
The new phone case is translucent enough to show the charging coil, which the design team spent four months making pretty.
words.etymology: trans-(穿过) + lucere(发光) → 光能透过 → 半透明

meanings.en: not giving enough attention to what you are doing, so that you make mistakes or cause damage
meanings.zh: 粗心的;疏忽的;不当心的

examples: One careless click on a fake invoice link, and the whole finance team spent the weekend resetting passwords and calling the bank.
He is careless with borrowed things: my drill came back with the case cracked and two bits missing from the tray.
The report was full of careless mistakes, including two wrong dates and a client's name misspelled, so my manager sent it back.
A careless driver left the van in neutral on the slope, and it rolled through the fence into the neighbor's flower beds.
It was careless of me to mention her salary at dinner, and the table went quiet for a very long ten seconds.

meanings.en: so great or so good that nothing else can be compared with it

examples: The tiny museum has unparalleled access to the family archive, so researchers fly in from three continents just to read letters.
Her second album sold four million copies in a month, an unparalleled run for a singer who was busking two years earlier.
Streaming gave the studio unparalleled data about which scene made viewers reach for the remote, down to the exact second.
The blackout caused unparalleled damage to the regional grid, and engineers still argue about which substation gave way first.
He speaks six languages and reads two more, an unparalleled asset in a newsroom that has to cover half the planet.
words.etymology: un-(无) + parallel(匹敌) → 无可匹敌

meanings.en: failing to give something the care or attention that a duty requires, so that harm results
meanings.zh: 玩忽职守的;失职的;疏忽的

examples: The court found the landlord negligent for ignoring six written complaints about the loose railing before the child fell.
A single negligent nurse left the drug cabinet unlocked overnight, and the whole ward spent Monday morning counting ampoules.
Insurers refused the claim, calling the driver negligent for texting at a junction he crossed twice a day.
He has been negligent about backups for years, then lost eleven months of client files to a dead drive on a Friday.
The report named three negligent inspectors who had signed off on welds they never actually looked at.
words.etymology: neg-(不) + legere(留意) → 不加留意 → 失职

meanings.en: happening now and then at irregular intervals, rather than steadily or predictably
meanings.zh: 零星的;偶发的;时断时续的

examples: Sporadic gunfire kept the aid convoy parked at the checkpoint for two days, even though the ceasefire was officially holding.
The app has sporadic outages every few weeks, always at lunchtime, and support blames a cache nobody will admit to owning.
Her attendance was sporadic after January, three classes one week and none the next, so the tutor finally called home.
Sporadic rain all afternoon ruined the outdoor tasting, and the caterers moved eighty guests into a garage full of bicycles.
We got sporadic updates from the expedition, a satellite message on Tuesday and then nothing until the following Sunday.
words.etymology: 希腊 sporas(散落的) → 零星散布

meanings.en: an official order issued by a ruler, government, or court that has the force of law
to order something officially, using the authority of law

examples: A presidential decree closed the border at midnight, and families who had shopped across it for decades were suddenly stuck.
The judge's decree gave her the house and him the vineyard, ending a divorce that had run for four years.
By decree, every street sign in the capital had to be repainted blue, a job that outlasted the mayor who ordered it.
Only a monarch could decree a public holiday at such short notice, and the shops had eleven hours to get ready.
The council decreed that no building on the harbor front may rise above four floors, and the developer sued that same week.
words.etymology: de-(向下) + cernere(裁断) → 自上而下的裁令

meanings.en: the formal act of announcing a law or regulation so that it officially comes into force
the act of spreading a belief or doctrine so that it becomes widely known

examples: The promulgation of the new privacy rules gave companies ninety days to rewrite consent forms they had used since 2015.
Nothing changed on the ground for a year after the promulgation of the labor code, because no inspector was ever hired.
Historians date the modern state to the promulgation of the 1947 constitution, not to the surrender that came before it.
The ministry timed the promulgation for a Friday evening, hoping the weekend would swallow the coverage entirely.
The order's whole purpose was the promulgation of one idea, and its monks carried it across four kingdoms on foot.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + vulgus(民众) → 推向民众 → 公布

meanings.en: full of danger, so that serious harm or failure is a real possibility

examples: The last mile to the summit is perilous in April, when meltwater loosens rock the guidebooks still describe as solid.
Crossing the strait in a rubber boat is perilous even in summer, and the coast guard logs a rescue most weekends.
The company's cash position looked perilous by October: two months of payroll left and a client who paid at ninety days.
She took a perilous shortcut through the quarry to make her shift, and her bike came home with a bent fork.
Reporting from the border turned perilous once both sides began treating a press vest as a target rather than protection.
words.etymology: 拉丁 periculum(危险) → 充满危险

meanings.en: in almost the same way, or used to introduce a second case that resembles the first

examples: The London office cut its travel budget in March; the Berlin team similarly grounded everyone except two account leads.
Chili flakes bloom better in hot oil, and dried herbs behave similarly, so add them before the tomatoes go in.
Her first novel took nine years; the second, written on trains between hospital visits, arrived similarly slowly.
The old model overheated after twenty minutes of video, and the replacement performs similarly once the room passes thirty degrees.
Free shipping lifted weekend orders by a fifth. Similarly, the loyalty discount moved Tuesday sales, though only for coffee.
words.etymology: similis(相像) → 以相像的方式

meanings.en: so shocking or morally offensive that it disgusts you
meanings.zh: 令人作呕的;令人愤慨的

meanings.en: making you feel physically ill or about to vomit
meanings.zh: 令人恶心的;使人反胃的

examples: There was a sickening thud from the stairwell, and every phone in the office came out at once.
The documentary shows sickening conditions at the shelter: forty dogs, one volunteer, and a vet bill nobody had paid since spring.
He read the group chat and felt a sickening drop in his stomach; they had been planning the trip without him for weeks.
The bus lurched around the mountain switchbacks with a sickening roll that emptied half the seats at the first rest stop.
It is sickening to hear a company call eleven hundred layoffs a rebalancing while the chairman collects a record bonus.

meanings.en: matching something else in size, degree, or seriousness, so that the two stay in balance
meanings.zh: 成比例的;相称的;适度的

examples: The fine has to be proportionate to the harm done, so a lost password and a leaked medical file cannot cost the same.
Tenants pay a proportionate share of the heating bill, worked out by floor area rather than by how many radiators they own.
Police called the response proportionate; the video, watched forty million times by Sunday, persuaded very few people of that.
Give each region a proportionate number of delegates, or the smallest province will keep vetoing budgets it barely funds.
Her workload grew every quarter without any proportionate rise in pay, so she left for a competitor in October.
words.etymology: pro-(依照) + portio(份额) → 按份额相称

meanings.en: following a slow, winding course instead of a direct line
going on at length without a clear direction or point

examples: A meandering stream cuts the field into three awkward pieces, which is why the farm has never sold well at auction.
His meandering answer took four minutes and never once touched the question the reporter had actually asked.
We took the meandering coast road instead of the motorway and arrived three hours late with a car full of sand.
The novel opens with sixty pages of meandering childhood memory before anything resembling a plot finally arrives.
Their meandering Sunday walks always ended at the same bakery, whatever route the dog had chosen on the way.
words.etymology: 希腊 Maiandros(以曲折著称的河) → 蜿蜒

meanings.en: to take money or property from someone by deceiving them

examples: Prosecutors say the pair set up nine shell companies to defraud elderly clients of nearly two million dollars.
He was jailed for four years after defrauding the pension fund he had managed since leaving the navy.
The scheme was simple enough to defraud a bank twice: the same invoice, two branches, three weeks apart.
She realized her landlord had defrauded her when the deposit protection service had no record of the account.
Anyone who tries to defraud the disaster fund will be prosecuted, the governor said, even for amounts under a hundred dollars.
words.etymology: de-(夺去) + fraus(欺骗) → 骗走

meanings.en: unhappily wanting something that someone else has, such as their success or possessions

examples: She posted the promotion at midnight and woke to forty congratulations, three of which were plainly envious.
I am envious of anyone who can sleep on a plane; I arrive after eleven hours looking like a hostage.
The team was less envious than baffled that a junior hire got the corner desk in her second week.
He shot an envious look at the neighbor's new greenhouse, then spent the whole weekend rebuilding his own cold frame.
Being envious of a friend's marriage is a poor guide to your own; you only ever see the parts they publish.
words.etymology: in-(朝) + videre(看) → 斜眼盯着 → 嫉妒

meanings.en: inclined to disagree and to keep debating, often in a way others find tiring

examples: Two glasses of wine and he turns argumentative, picking apart the parking policy with people who only wanted dessert.
The teacher's note called him argumentative, which his mother read as a compliment and his father read as a warning.
Reviewers found the book argumentative rather than persuasive, as if the author expected a fight on every page.
She is argumentative in meetings and unfailingly kind afterwards, which confuses everyone who has only seen her at work.
An argumentative comment thread under a recipe for banana bread ran to four hundred replies before the site shut it.
words.etymology: arguere(辩明,论证) → 事事要辩

meanings.en: to tell someone firmly that you disapprove of what they have done
to urge someone earnestly to do something, as a warning for their own good

examples: The judge admonished the lawyer for checking his phone during testimony, then let the hearing continue as if nothing had happened.
Her grandmother would admonish anyone who left the tap running, including guests who had driven four hours to visit.
The memo admonishes staff to log every visitor, a rule invented after a stranger spent a whole afternoon in the server room.
He was admonished twice in one shift, once for the uniform and once for a joke the supervisor overheard in the corridor.
Coaches admonish young pitchers to rest their arms, and young pitchers, being nineteen, mostly ignore them until something tears.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + monere(提醒) → 提醒并责备

meanings.en: to be in charge of work or a process and make sure it is done properly

examples: She was hired to oversee the move to the new warehouse, and finished it three weeks early with the same crew.
Two auditors now oversee every payment above ten thousand euros, a rule the board added after the invoice scandal.
Nobody wanted to oversee the summer interns, so the job went to whoever came back from lunch last on Monday.
The agency oversees eleven hundred kilometers of track and cannot say how many bridges it has actually inspected this decade.
He will oversee quality on the factory floor, which mostly means walking the line twice a day and asking blunt questions.
words.etymology: over-(在上) + see(看) → 在上面看管

meanings.en: to weaken something or make it work less well than it should

examples: Two nights of bad sleep impair judgment more than most drivers realize, which is why the haulage firm now tracks rest hours.
The infection can impair hearing permanently if antibiotics start more than a week late.
