Salt from the winter roads impairs the sensors, so the car brakes for shadows until someone hoses out the wheel arches.
Nothing in the contract may impair the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment, however the clause about noise is worded.
A cracked lens impaired the telescope for eight months, and the repair mission cost more than the original build.
words.etymology: im-(使) + pejor(更坏) → 使变坏

meanings.en: extremely unpleasant or annoying, especially in a rude, loud, or offensive way
meanings.zh: 令人讨厌的;可憎的;粗鲁烦人的

examples: The new sales hire seemed friendly on Zoom, but in the office he turned obnoxious, shouting into his headset and mocking everyone's lunch.
Our upstairs neighbor plays obnoxious bass-heavy music until two in the morning, then leaves passive-aggressive notes when the baby cries at seven.
The free version of the app is unusable now, with obnoxious full-screen ads popping up between every level of the game.
One obnoxious passenger held up the whole boarding line, filming himself arguing with the gate agent about his oversized carry-on.
Mute the group chat during election week; a few relatives get so obnoxious that even the family peacemaker stops replying.
words.etymology: ob-(对着) + noxa(伤害) → 招人厌恶

meanings.en: to secretly plan with other people to do something harmful, illegal, or sneaky
(of events or circumstances) to combine as if by design to produce a bad result
meanings.zh: (事情)凑到一起(造成不良后果)

examples: Prosecutors say the three executives conspired over encrypted chats to fix prices before the merger was even announced.
Her roommates conspired for weeks to plan the surprise party, deleting messages whenever she borrowed anyone's phone.
Two moderators conspired with a seller to bury negative reviews, and the forum's entire ranking system lost credibility overnight.
A canceled train, a dead phone battery, and a sudden downpour conspired to make her miss the only interview she cared about.
Rising rents and shrinking grants conspire against small theaters, closing three of them in our neighborhood this year alone.
words.etymology: con-(共同) + spirare(呼吸) → 同声共气,密谋

meanings.en: to gradually weaken someone's authority, confidence, or the success of an effort, often in a hidden way
to dig beneath something or wear away its base so that it may collapse
meanings.zh: 在……底下挖掘;侵蚀……的基础

examples: By publicly questioning each decision in meetings, the deputy slowly undermined the new manager without ever raising his voice.
Leaked screenshots of the deleted safety report undermine the company's claim that it knew nothing before the recall.
Constant comparison with filtered photos can undermine a teenager's confidence long before anyone says a single unkind word.
Skipping the cheap maintenance now will undermine everything the migration achieved, and we will be back to weekend outages by December.
Decades of storm waves have undermined the cliff path, so the council moved the fence ten meters inland this spring.
words.etymology: under(下面) + mine(挖坑道) → 挖空根基

meanings.en: to become smaller or less, or to make something smaller or less
to make someone or something seem less important or valuable than they really are

examples: Battery capacity diminishes a little every winter, and by year four the car barely covers the school run without a midday charge.
The painkillers diminish the swelling within an hour, but the physio warned him not to train on a numb ankle.
Streaming did not kill radio, but it steadily diminished the audience until the station cut the morning show to two hours.
As the wildfire smoke cleared, the crowd's fear diminished, and vendors began reopening their stalls along the waterfront.
Calling her promotion luck diminishes ten years of unpaid overtime, and she finally said so in front of the whole team.
words.etymology: di-(向下,即de-) + minuere(变小) → 减少

meanings.en: unable to understand or explain something; completely confused

examples: Engineers were baffled for a week by the server crashing at 3 a.m. daily, until someone noticed the backup job's timezone.
The vet admitted she was baffled: the dog's bloodwork looked perfect, yet he refused every meal for five straight days.
Economists remain baffled that prices keep climbing while warehouses sit full, and every forecast this quarter has missed badly.
My grandmother stared at the QR-code menu, utterly baffled, until the waiter quietly brought her a laminated paper copy.
Detectives were openly baffled by the museum theft; the alarms never tripped, and the cameras recorded nothing but an empty hallway.

meanings.en: to move someone or something down to a lower rank, or to a less important position or role
meanings.zh: 把…降级;使贬至次要地位

meanings.en: (mainly British) to move a sports team down to a lower division after a poor season
meanings.zh: 使(球队)降入低级别联赛

examples: After the merger, the redesign that had consumed her whole year was relegated to a footnote in the investor deck.
The settings menu relegates the privacy controls to a third-level submenu, which critics say is no accident.
Once the baby arrived, the treadmill was relegated to the garage, where it now serves as a coat rack.
Two losses in the final week were enough to relegate the club to the second division for the first time in forty years.
Fans stormed the boardroom meeting after the team was relegated on the season's last day, blaming the owner's refusal to spend in January.
words.etymology: re-(远离) + legare(派遣) → 打发到次要位置

meanings.en: expressed or styled in a deliberately restrained way, avoiding show or exaggeration
meanings.zh: 低调的;克制的;不张扬的

examples: The hotel lobby is all understated luxury: pale oak, soft lamps, and not a single logo in sight.
Her acceptance speech was so understated that half the audience missed the announcement that she was retiring.
The watch costs more than a car, but its understated dial looks like something you might find at a flea market.
Reviewers praised the actor's understated performance, saying a single tired glance carried more grief than any monologue could.
The startup's understated launch — one blog post, no press tour — somehow generated more buzz than its rivals' stadium events.
words.etymology: under-(不足) + state(陈述) → 说得轻、不张扬

meanings.en: a law or rule made by a city or local government, applying only within its area
a religious ceremony or practice that a church directs its members to observe, such as baptism

examples: The city council passed an ordinance banning gas-powered leaf blowers, and landscapers have until March to switch to electric.
A noise ordinance shuts the patio speakers off at ten, so the bar moved its live music indoors.
Short-term rentals exploded downtown until a zoning ordinance capped them at ninety nights a year per host.
He got a ticket for feeding pigeons, and only then learned the ordinance had been on the books since 1987.
The mayor vetoed the sidewalk-vending ordinance, arguing it would push food carts into neighborhoods with no foot traffic.
words.etymology: ordin-(秩序) + -ance(名词) → 定秩序的法令

meanings.en: to follow a winding, indirect course, or to wander slowly with no fixed direction
(of talk, writing, or thought) to drift from topic to topic without a clear point
meanings.zh: (讲话、文章)东拉西扯,漫无主题

meanings.en: a bend or winding curve in a river, path, or road

examples: The trail meanders along the river for six kilometers, so runners chasing a fast time take the highway path instead.
We had no itinerary in Lisbon, just three days to meander through the old quarters and follow whatever smelled like fresh bread.
Delivery drivers hate the new suburb because its streets meander in loops designed to slow traffic, adding ten minutes per drop.
The keynote meandered from supply chains to the speaker's sailing trip, and by minute forty nobody remembered the product being launched.
From the drone, each meander of the river showed as a bright loop, with old cut-off bends fading into marsh beside it.
words.etymology: Maiandros(古河名,河道极曲折) → 蜿蜒

meanings.en: a serious piece of advice or a mild warning telling someone how they should or should not behave

examples: The onboarding deck ends with a stern admonition never to share credentials over chat, which someone violates in week one every single cohort.
Despite the judge's admonition to stay off social media, the defendant posted about the trial before the jury even left the building.
Her grandmother's admonition about saving three months of rent felt quaint until the layoffs hit and it suddenly sounded like prophecy.
The lifeguard's whistle came with an admonition to stop diving in the shallow end, delivered loudly enough for the whole pool to hear.
Analysts read the central bank's statement as an admonition against reckless lending, though it named no bank in particular.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + monere(警告) → 告诫

meanings.en: an official public announcement about something important, or the act of making one

examples: The mayor signed a proclamation declaring June bike-to-work month, then rode home in a downpour that delighted the photographers.
The CEO's return-to-office proclamation landed at 4:59 on a Friday, and the reply-all thread kept HR busy through the weekend.
Visitors line up to see the yellowed proclamation that freed the state's last enslaved people, displayed under glass beside the governor's pen.
Every diet he starts arrives with a proclamation on Instagram, and every quiet burger afterward goes unphotographed.
The governor's emergency proclamation released flood funds hours before the river crested behind the elementary school.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + clamare(呼喊) → 公开宣告

meanings.en: so bad, cruel, or offensive that it deserves to be hated

examples: The landlord's habit of showing the apartment without notice was detestable, but the below-market rent kept everyone politely silent.
Charging families extra to sit with their own children on a flight struck even the airline's staff as detestable.
He plays a detestable tech founder so convincingly that strangers scold him in coffee shops between seasons.
Scam calls that target grandparents with fake arrest warrants are detestable in a way ordinary spam never quite manages.
The comment section turned detestable within an hour of the verdict, so the editor closed it and logged off early.
words.etymology: de-(向下) + testari(作证) → 立誓诅咒→可憎

meanings.en: involving careful digging into facts and evidence, especially to expose wrongdoing

examples: An investigative reporter spent eight months tracing the charity's donations to a shell company registered above a vape shop.
The podcast's investigative series on nursing-home staffing forced the state to audit forty facilities before the season even ended.
She left corporate law for investigative work at a consumer watchdog, trading billable hours for freedom-of-information requests.
The insurer's investigative unit flagged the claim after noticing the stolen laptop still pinging a café's Wi-Fi every morning.
The documentary crew took an investigative approach, filing records requests instead of accepting the ministry's carefully guided factory tour.
words.etymology: in-(进入) + vestigium(足迹) → 循足迹追查

meanings.en: light, playful talk in which people tease each other in a friendly way
to exchange playful, teasing remarks with someone

examples: The morning stand-up runs on ten minutes of banter before anyone mentions a ticket, and honestly the team ships faster for it.
Their podcast is mostly banter about lunch orders and video games, with the actual film review squeezed into the last five minutes.
New hires mistake the kitchen banter for a real argument until they notice both engineers grinning over their coffee.
The broadcast lost its charm once the two commentators dropped their banter and started reading sponsor scripts at each other.
The barber and his oldest customer banter about the same three headlines every visit, and neither would change a word of it.

meanings.en: confident, stylish, and charming in an easy, polished way, usually said of men
meanings.zh: 温文尔雅的；潇洒迷人的(多形容男子)

examples: The hotel concierge stayed debonair through the fire alarm, guiding guests outside as if he were hosting a garden party.
Investors expected a nervous founder, but he walked into the pitch debonair in a linen suit, cracking jokes about his own burn rate.
My grandfather looks impossibly debonair in the 1962 photo, tilted hat and thin tie, waiting outside the dance hall.
The airline's new ads feature a debonair pilot winking at the camera, a throwback style the marketing team calls the golden age of travel.
Even on a video call from a messy kitchen, the actor managed to seem debonair, scarf knotted just so.
words.etymology: de(从) + bon(好) + aire(出身、性情) → 风度翩翩

meanings.en: having or involving many casual sexual partners
mixing things together carelessly, without choosing or selecting; indiscriminate

examples: The documentary follows dating-app culture without judging anyone as promiscuous, though the comment section had no such restraint.
Public-health workers stress that the outbreak spreads through networks, not morals, and that labeling patients promiscuous only keeps them from getting tested.
Tabloids painted the young singer as promiscuous over a few blurry club photos, and her lawyers responded within a day.
Set the network card to promiscuous mode and it captures every packet on the segment, not just traffic addressed to it.
Critics called the museum's new wing a promiscuous jumble of styles, Gothic arches crashing into glass curtain walls.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + miscere(混合) → 混杂不加选择

meanings.en: looking or sounding very sad, as if grieving; often used of sounds, faces, and places
meanings.zh: 哀伤的；(声音、神情、气氛)凄婉的

examples: The last freight train crosses at midnight, and its mournful whistle carries across the whole valley when the air is cold.
The shelter posted a photo of the old beagle's mournful eyes, and applications to adopt him tripled overnight.
A lone busker played something slow and mournful on the cello, and the whole subway platform went quiet for a minute.
Wind through the abandoned lighthouse makes a low, mournful sound that tour guides swear is not part of the recording.
The goalkeeper gave one mournful look at the scoreboard before trudging off, and the cameras stayed on him the whole way.
words.etymology: mourn(哀悼) + -ful(充满……的) → 哀伤的

meanings.en: full of deep sadness or grief; a literary word for profound, personal sorrow
meanings.zh: 悲痛的；哀切的(多用于书面语)

examples: Her memoir's final chapter is openly sorrowful, written the winter her brother's chair at the table finally stood empty.
The war photographer said the hardest shot was not the rubble but one sorrowful mother sorting school uniforms that no one would wear.
The novel ends on a sorrowful note: the letters arrive a week after the funeral, still smelling of her tobacco.
Museum visitors linger longest at the sorrowful last diary entry, three lines a girl wrote the night before the ship went down.
He kept his father's watch wound for years, a small sorrowful ritual he never mentioned to anyone at work.
words.etymology: sorrow(悲伤) + -ful(充满……的) → 哀痛的

meanings.en: showing kindness and understanding toward someone who is suffering or having a hard time
inclined to approve of and support a person, idea, or cause
meanings.zh: (对想法、事业、人)支持的,赞同的

examples: The nurse gave him a sympathetic look and stayed past her shift so he wouldn't hear the test results alone.
When my flight got cancelled, the gate agent was sympathetic but honest: nothing was leaving that airport before morning.
Her manager was sympathetic about the burnout, cutting her meeting load in half instead of just recommending a meditation app.
Several board members are sympathetic to the four-day-week proposal, though none will say so publicly before the pilot data comes in.
The judge seemed sympathetic to the startup's argument that the patent was too vague to enforce against anyone.
words.etymology: sym-(共同) + path(感受) → 感同身受

meanings.en: willing to listen to and consider new ideas, suggestions, or offers
meanings.zh: 乐于接受的;愿意倾听(新想法、建议)的

examples: Pitch the redesign on Friday afternoon; the director is far more receptive once the week's fires are already out.
Investors were surprisingly receptive to the founder's admission that the first product had failed, reading it as honesty rather than weakness.
Teenagers are more receptive to advice from a coach they respect than to the same words repeated by their parents.
The city council proved receptive to the bike-lane petition after 3,000 residents signed it in a single weekend.
Keep the demo short: an audience stays receptive for about ten minutes, then every extra slide costs you goodwill.
words.etymology: re-(回) + cept(拿取) → 愿意接纳

meanings.en: made up of people and influences from many different countries; international in character
meanings.zh: 国际化的;汇聚多元文化的

meanings.en: (of a person) at home in many cultures through wide travel and experience, free of narrow local attitudes
meanings.zh: 见多识广的;四海为家的

examples: Lisbon has grown so cosmopolitan that my street now has a Nepali grocery, a Brazilian bakery, and three coworking spaces full of remote workers.
The airline's ads sell Dubai as a cosmopolitan hub where forty nationalities share one office tower and nobody counts as a foreigner.
Compared with the capital's cosmopolitan food scene, this town offers two diners and a gas station that closes at nine.
Years of postings in Nairobi, Seoul, and Lima made her genuinely cosmopolitan, able to read a room in any language.
He cultivates a cosmopolitan image online, but his passport shows one stamp and his palate stops at pizza.

relatedForms.zh: 世界主义;四海一家的观念

words.etymology: cosmo(世界) + polites(公民) → 世界公民般的

meanings.en: the attempt to settle a dispute by having a neutral third party help both sides reach an agreement

examples: The landlord and tenants agreed to mediation after six months of certified letters had produced nothing but thicker files.
HR proposed mediation between the two engineers before their feud could split the whole platform team into camps.
Divorce mediation cost them a tenth of what a courtroom battle would have, and the kids never had to testify to anyone.
Qatar's mediation between the two governments produced a ceasefire draft that neither side loved and both could sign.
The contract sends every billing dispute to mediation first, so nobody sees a judge until a neutral has tried for thirty days.
words.etymology: medi(中间) + -ation(行为) → 居中调停

meanings.en: badly planned or messy, with no clear order or system
meanings.zh: 杂乱无章的;缺乏条理的

examples: The onboarding was so disorganized that three new hires spent their first week without laptops, badges, or a manager who knew they existed.
Her desk looks disorganized, yet she can pull any receipt from the pile in under ten seconds.
Investors walked out early because the pitch was disorganized, jumping from pricing to hiring before anyone explained the product.
The relief effort stayed disorganized for days, with two agencies delivering water to the same town while a third got nothing.
He is brilliant but disorganized, so his calendar is triple-booked and his tax documents live in a shoebox.

meanings.en: an earnest, often emotional request that someone do something

examples: Despite the drivers' repeated entreaties, the company kept the routing algorithm that sent them through flooded streets.
Her final entreaty to the landlord, a handwritten letter about twelve years of on-time rent, went unanswered for a month.
The coach ignored every entreaty to rest the injured striker, and the decision ended the team's season by November.
Fans flooded the studio with entreaties to keep the show's original composer after the reboot trailer dropped.
He made one last entreaty at the border office, holding up photos of the family he had not seen in years.

meanings.en: public support for a cause, policy, or group, argued for actively

examples: Years of advocacy by cyclists finally convinced the council to protect the bike lanes with concrete instead of paint.
The nonprofit's advocacy shifted from street protests to drafting model legislation that three states later adopted almost word for word.
Her advocacy for plain-language contracts began after watching her parents sign a loan they never understood.
The hospital hired a patient advocacy team after complaints that billing questions took months to resolve.
His advocacy of remote work predates the pandemic by a decade, back when it cost him a promotion.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + vocare(呼喊) → 替人发声

meanings.en: continuing for the whole of a person's life

examples: Her lifelong fear of open water finally cracked at forty, when a patient instructor got her floating in a hotel pool.
He describes himself as a lifelong fan, though he only started watching the team after they signed the Brazilian striker.
The summer scholarship turned a holiday job into a lifelong career, and she still writes to the professor who nominated her.
Two strangers seated together on a delayed flight to Lisbon struck up a conversation that became a lifelong friendship.
Learning is meant to be lifelong, yet almost all of our training budget disappears on people under thirty.
words.etymology: life(一生) + long(长久) → 持续一生的

meanings.en: a false spoken statement that damages someone's reputation
to damage someone's reputation by saying false things about them

examples: The chef sued a rival for slander after a voice note accusing him of reusing oil spread through the restaurant group.
Calling it criticism does not help; naming a colleague as a thief in front of clients is slander.
He slandered the outgoing treasurer at three separate meetings, and the minutes now read like a court case waiting to happen.
Anonymous accounts slander candidates in the final week of a campaign, betting that a correction will arrive too late to matter.
Her lawyer drew a careful line between an unflattering review and slander, and the paper's editors relaxed for the first time in weeks.
words.etymology: scandalum(绊脚石;丑闻) → 中伤的言辞

meanings.en: widely known and admired for some special quality or achievement

examples: The clinic is renowned for reattaching fingers, and surgeons fly in from three continents to watch a single morning of operations.
She is renowned among translators for refusing any deadline that would force her to skip a second reading.
A renowned violin teacher moved into the village, and within a year the primary school had a waiting list.
The festival was once renowned for its lineup and is now renowned for its queues and its eleven-dollar water.
Being renowned in a narrow field means four hundred people know your name and nobody else has ever heard of you.
words.etymology: re-(再) + nomer(称呼) → 被反复提起的

meanings.en: not known to most people, or difficult to understand
meanings.zh: 鲜为人知的;晦涩难懂的

meanings.en: to make something difficult to see, hear, or understand

examples: The album stayed an obscure import until a video app turned its third track into a fifteen-second sound.
His answer was so obscure that two lawyers left the room disagreeing about what he had actually promised.
Fog obscured the runway lights, and the pilot circled twice before diverting to an airport ninety kilometers north.
A confident headline can obscure a report's actual finding, especially when the finding is boring and the headline is not.
She built a career on obscure nineteenth-century diaries that nobody else had ever bothered to digitize.
words.etymology: ob-(遮住) + scurus(覆盖) → 被盖住,看不清

meanings.en: complete destruction, so that nothing of something remains

examples: The general spoke of annihilation as if it were a logistics problem, and two aides quietly asked to be reassigned.
These reefs face annihilation within a decade unless the water stops warming, the survey's authors write in unusually blunt language.
What began as a friendly rematch ended in annihilation: nine goals, two red cards, and a manager resigning at midnight.
Physicists photograph the annihilation of a particle and its antiparticle, a flash lasting far less than a blink.
He talks about the annihilation of his savings the way other people describe weather, calmly and without any plan.
words.etymology: ad-(到) + nihil(无) → 化为乌有

meanings.en: to destroy something so completely that nothing recognizable is left
to cover or wipe out something so that it can no longer be seen or remembered

examples: One overnight flood obliterated the ground floor of the archive, and forty years of case files became pulp.
The new tower obliterates the view that made the terrace worth its rent, and half the tenants are leaving.
A single misplaced command can obliterate a production database, which is why the deploy script now asks twice.
Rain obliterated the chalk markings before the second heat, so the officials remeasured the whole course by tape.
She wanted to obliterate that year from memory, but the photos kept surfacing in a helpfully automated slideshow.
words.etymology: ob-(相反) + littera(字母) → 把字抹掉

meanings.en: an angry argument or disagreement, usually between people who know each other well
to argue angrily with someone

examples: The brothers had a quarrel over their mother's kitchen table and did not speak to each other for nine years.
I have no quarrel with the plan itself; my objection is that nobody has costed the second year.
They quarreled about the thermostat every winter until one of them bought a second blanket and stopped mentioning it.
A petty quarrel about seating arrangements delayed the signing by two hours and made every front page the next morning.
Neighbors quarrel over parking spaces on this street with an energy that could power a small municipality.
words.etymology: querela(抱怨;控诉) → 争吵

meanings.en: to argue noisily about something trivial
a noisy argument about something unimportant

examples: Two departments squabbled for a month over who owned the shared inbox, and the customers waited.
The board meeting collapsed into a squabble about biscuits, which is how a surprising number of them end.
Children squabble over the window seat, and the adults have simply moved that same argument into email.
A petty squabble between two coalition partners froze the housing bill for an entire parliamentary session.
They squabbled at the checkout about expired coupons while the queue behind them grew to eleven people.

meanings.en: to feel angry or bitter about something because you think it is unfair

examples: She resents being the only person on the team who remembers to reorder the coffee.
Long-serving staff resent the new job title far more than the salary attached to it, which surprised nobody in HR.
He says he does not resent his brother's success, then changes the subject with impressive speed.
Voters resent being told the economy is fine while their grocery bill climbs every single month.
I resent the assumption that whoever answers the phone is also the person who will make the tea.
words.etymology: re-(反过来) + sentire(感觉) → 心里泛起的恶感

meanings.en: a feeling of resentment kept alive long after the event that caused it
to give or allow something unwillingly

examples: He has held a grudge since the 2019 seating plan, and every team lunch is quietly shaped by it.
Small towns keep a grudge the way cities keep records: indefinitely, and with excellent recall of the details.
She bears no grudge against the manager who let her go, mostly because the next job paid nearly double.
It was billed as a friendly, but two red cards in twenty minutes made it obvious this was a grudge match.
He grudges every minute spent on paperwork, though he will happily spend an hour choosing a font.

meanings.en: the state of having plenty of money and material comfort

examples: The suburb wears its affluence quietly: no gates, no gold, just very good trees and very silent streets.
Rising affluence in the region changed what the supermarket stocked long before it changed how anyone voted.
Her novels examine affluence from the inside, which is why critics who grew up rich find them so uncomfortable.
There is a particular loneliness that arrives with affluence, and the clinic's waiting list is full of it.
Affluence did not make his commute any shorter; it only made the car in which he sat much nicer.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + fluere(流) → 财富源源流来

meanings.en: completely still, without any movement at all

examples: The heron stood motionless in the shallows for eleven minutes, then struck once and swallowed a fish whole.
He sat motionless through the entire verdict, and only his hands on the rail gave anything away.
Traffic was motionless on the bridge, so half the bus emptied out and walked the last kilometer.
The lizard stays motionless on the warm brick until a shadow crosses it, and then it is simply gone.
She held the pose motionless while the old printer warmed up, and the whole studio held its breath with her.

meanings.en: to make someone very interested and curious about something
meanings.zh: 激起…的好奇心;引起兴趣

meanings.en: secret plotting, especially inside a government or an organization

examples: The job listing intrigued her mainly because it refused to name the company anywhere in eight paragraphs.
What intrigues economists about the town is that everyone left, and then, ten years later, half of them came back.
Palace intrigue fills the memoir's middle chapters, though the author insists she was only ever taking notes.
The gallery's mislabeled painting continues to intrigue researchers who have no funding and no intention of stopping.
Two decades of office intrigue ended the afternoon the founder sold the building and everyone was suddenly remote.
words.etymology: in-(进入) + tricae(纠缠) → 使人陷入纠葛

meanings.en: to plot or scheme secretly in order to bring about something harmful

examples: Two deputy directors machinated for months to have the audit quietly reassigned to a friendlier office.
He machinates the way other people garden: patiently, in small weekly increments, and always before anyone notices.
The novel's villains machinate over dinner while the servants, who understand everything, silently refill the glasses.
Nobody needed to machinate; the committee was perfectly capable of destroying the proposal on its own.
She insists she does not machinate, though her calendar shows four private meetings before every board vote.
words.etymology: machina(机械;装置) → 设计机关,谋划

meanings.en: to drive back or force away an attack or an attacker
to make someone feel strong dislike or disgust
(of a surface or a force) to keep something away instead of absorbing or attracting it

examples: The garrison managed to repel three assaults before dawn, then found that the fourth had come through a service tunnel.
His theory of networking repels everyone he meets, which he takes as proof that the theory is ahead of its time.
The jacket will repel rain for exactly one season, after which it becomes an expensive sponge with a good logo.
Something in the tone of the message repelled her, though every individual sentence in it was perfectly polite.
Magnets repel each other when you turn one around, which is the only physics my nephew currently accepts.
words.etymology: re-(回) + pellere(推) → 推回去

meanings.en: to reject an offer, request, or friendly gesture in a blunt or unkind way
a blunt rejection of an offer or an approach

examples: The label chose to rebuff her demo twice, then signed her in a hurry after a bootleg clip went viral.
Every attempt to open a back channel met the same polite rebuff, delivered by the same unhurried deputy.
He rebuffs invitations so consistently that his friends now simply announce their plans instead of asking.
The rebuff stung less than the delay: four weeks of silence, and then two lines from an assistant.
She had prepared for a rebuff and got an enthusiastic yes, which left her without a second sentence.
words.etymology: re-(回) + buffo(冲击) → 顶回去

meanings.en: annoyance or irritation, especially the kind caused by ongoing petty trouble
the act of making a bad situation or condition worse

examples: Renewing the permit is three forms and one afternoon of aggravation, and the office closes for lunch without warning.
He quit not over pay but over the daily aggravation of a system that logged him out every nine minutes.
The report blames the aggravation of the flooding on twenty years of paving over the flood plain.
Sending a second reminder saved us a week of aggravation and cost exactly one line of text.
Her doctor warned that the aggravation of the injury would come from the stairs, not from the gym.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + gravis(沉重) → 加重份量

meanings.en: strong public criticism or an open expression of disapproval
an official ruling that someone is guilty or that a building is unfit for use
meanings.zh: 定罪;(建筑)判定不宜使用

examples: The statement drew condemnation from three governments before most of the country had finished breakfast.
Universal condemnation is easy to write and, as the last two years showed, extremely easy to ignore.
Her condemnation of the practice was measured, sourced, and delivered without a single raised syllable.
The building's condemnation surprised nobody who had used the back stairs at any point in the last decade.
Silence from the board read as approval, so the delayed condemnation convinced nobody when it finally arrived.
words.etymology: con-(加强) + damnare(判罪) → 宣告有罪

meanings.en: extremely annoying or unpleasant to be around, especially because of arrogance
meanings.zh: 令人无法忍受的;傲慢得讨厌的

examples: He became insufferable after the promotion, correcting people's grammar in a channel he had created for lunch orders.
The heat in that top-floor office is insufferable by eleven, and the one window opens four centimeters.
Winning made the team insufferable; losing, it turns out, makes them merely unpleasant.
She is insufferable about her marathon time and yet somehow still the person everyone wants at a dinner.
Two hours of insufferable small talk bought the contract, so he counted the whole evening as work.
words.etymology: in-(不) + sufferre(承受) → 承受不了的

meanings.en: extremely unpleasant and deserving to be hated

examples: Comparisons are odious, my grandmother said, and then compared my brother's grades with mine for twenty minutes.
The regulation itself was harmless; the odious part was the clause quietly protecting whoever had written it.
He was handed the odious task of telling forty people that their department no longer existed.
Nothing in the contract is illegal, though several clauses are odious enough that no lawyer will read them aloud.
She finds cheerful corporate language odious and answers every circling back with a single flat word.
words.etymology: odium(憎恨) → 招人憎恨的

meanings.en: causing strong disgust or hatred

examples: The smell rising from the drain was loathsome enough that the inspection ended at the door.
He plays a loathsome landlord so convincingly that strangers refuse to sit near him on trains.
There is something loathsome about a company that thanks you warmly while deleting your account.
Cleaning the office fridge in August is loathsome work, and the rota has been mysteriously blank since June.
She described the practice as loathsome, then spent an hour explaining why it was also perfectly legal.
words.etymology: lāth(可憎的) + -some(令人…的) → 令人厌恶的

meanings.en: to gradually destroy or weaken something such as trust, support, or value
(of wind, water, or acid) to wear away rock, soil, or a surface over time

examples: Three quiet policy reversals eroded the trust it had taken the mayor two full terms to build.
Inflation will erode a fixed pension in a way that no single month ever makes obvious.
The river has eroded the bank so far that the fence at the bottom now ends in mid-air.
Repeated exceptions erode a rule faster than any argument against it ever could.
Salt spray erodes the bolts on the pier, and the council quietly replaces them every second summer.
words.etymology: e-(出) + rodere(啃咬) → 一点点啃掉

meanings.en: to support or strengthen something that is weak or under pressure

examples: The company bolstered its cash position weeks before the rate rise, which now looks like foresight rather than luck.
Two independent labs bolster the finding, and a third has promised its results by spring.
She bolstered her case with fourteen pages of receipts, and the landlord settled before the hearing.
Nothing bolsters a nervous team like shipping something small on the very first day.
The grant is meant to bolster rural clinics, though most of it has so far reached three large hospitals.

meanings.en: to become steadily smaller in size, number, or strength

examples: Attendance dwindled from ninety to eleven over four months, and nobody sent a single email asking why.
Our savings dwindle a little every time the boiler makes that particular noise.
The queue outside the embassy dwindles by noon, which is useless information if you work mornings.
Supplies dwindled to two crates of water and a box of batteries before the road finally reopened.
Interest in the podcast began to dwindle the month he started reading his own advertisements aloud.

meanings.en: (of a question or an examination) meant to uncover the truth, even when that is uncomfortable

examples: One probing question about the timeline collapsed a story the committee had accepted for two years.
She asks probing questions in the friendliest voice imaginable, which is exactly why people answer them.
The documentary is affectionate rather than probing, and the family clearly approved every single frame.
A probing internal review traced the fault to a checklist nobody had updated since the merger.
He met the probing follow-up with a joke, and the whole room noticed that he had not answered.
words.etymology: probare(检验) → 深入探查的

meanings.en: (of talk or tone) playfully teasing, with no intention of causing hurt

examples: Their bantering exchange across the counter is the only reason half the regulars come in before eight.
He kept a bantering tone through the whole negotiation, and every concession still went his way.
A bantering remark about the printer landed badly, because the printer had in fact just been replaced.
The interview stays bantering for ten minutes, then turns serious the moment the funding comes up.
She misses the bantering emails from the old team, which no group chat has ever managed to replace.

meanings.en: feeling and showing sympathy for people who are suffering, and wanting to help them
meanings.zh: 有同情心的;富有怜悯的

examples: The ward's most compassionate nurse is also its strictest, and nobody there has ever found that a contradiction.
He was granted compassionate leave and came back three days early because the house was simply too quiet.
A compassionate refusal is still a refusal, but people remember for years which kind they received.
Her compassionate reading of the case persuaded a judge who had already written half the opposite ruling.
Being compassionate at scale is hard: a thousand claims a week, and each one is somebody's worst month.
words.etymology: com-(共同) + pati(受苦) → 与人同受其苦

meanings.en: able to understand and share another person's feelings from the inside
meanings.zh: 有共情能力的;能设身处地的

examples: The most empathetic person in the room asked the one question nobody else had thought to ask.
Being empathetic is not the same as agreeing, and good mediators spend their careers in that gap.
Her empathetic reply took four sentences and defused a complaint that had been escalating for a week.
He is empathetic with strangers and strangely impatient with anyone he has known for over a decade.
An empathetic manager still has to deliver the bad number; the difference is the ten minutes afterwards.
words.etymology: en-(进入) + pathos(感受) → 进入他人的感受

meanings.en: to feel or express sorrow for someone else's trouble
to agree with or quietly support an opinion or a cause

examples: I sympathize with the night staff, though sympathy has not yet produced a second person on that desk.
She sympathized so convincingly that the caller ended up apologizing for having complained at all.
Many readers sympathize with the argument and not one of them intends to change what they buy.
It is easy to sympathize with the strikers when your own train is not the one being cancelled.
He sympathizes with both sides in the dispute, which each side has decided means he supports the other.
words.etymology: sym-(共同) + pathos(感受) → 与人共感

meanings.en: to publicly recommend or argue in favor of a policy, a course of action, or a group
someone who publicly supports a cause, or who speaks on another person's behalf

examples: Two of the three consultants advocate closing the smaller site, and the third has stopped attending the meetings.
She has advocated for cyclists at every council session since a van clipped her on the ring road.
The clinic assigns each patient an advocate who reads the forms that nobody else is ever going to read.
He advocates a four-day week in public and answers email at midnight on Sundays.
A tireless advocate of open data, she once mailed a printed spreadsheet to a minister who ignored her.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + vocare(呼喊) → 出面为人发声

meanings.en: to support or maintain a principle, standard, or decision
(of a court or authority) to confirm that an earlier decision was correct

examples: The union exists to uphold a standard that no individual member could ever enforce alone.
Appeals courts uphold most sentences, which is why the headline number of appeals means very little.
She upholds the old filing rules with a devotion that has outlasted three directors and one merger.
A referee who will not uphold a rule in minute eighty has effectively deleted it from the game.
The board voted to uphold the ban, then spent an hour discussing how to announce it kindly.

meanings.en: needing great physical effort and energy
(of an effort or an objection) determined and forcefully made

examples: The physiotherapist banned anything strenuous for six weeks, which he interpreted as permission to swim daily.
Strenuous objections from two departments delayed the rollout, and both objections turned out to be right.
A strenuous morning of moving boxes taught everyone which colleague actually goes to the gym.
Despite strenuous denials, the timeline in the leaked calendar matched the version the reporters had printed.
She made a strenuous case for the smaller budget and lost narrowly to a slide with a bigger number.

meanings.en: a person, organization or channel that passes information, money or influence from one party to another
a pipe or tube that carries water, or a protective channel enclosing electrical cables

examples: For eighteen months the intern was the only conduit between the sales floor and a CEO who never read email.
Prosecutors argued the shell company was simply a conduit, moving donations through three countries before they reached the campaign.
The electrician spent Saturday running fresh cable through the metal conduit above the ceiling tiles in our new office.
A leaking conduit under the car park flooded the basement gym twice, and management blamed the tenants both times.
Group chats have become the main conduit for neighborhood rumors, which arrive faster and less accurately than the local paper.
words.etymology: con-(共同) + ducere(引导) → 引流的管道

meanings.en: strong disagreement with a plan or policy, and the actions taken to resist it
the main political party or parties not in government
the team or person you are competing against

examples: Fierce opposition from parents killed the plan to move the school day forward by ninety minutes.
The landlord withdrew the rent increase after four months of organized opposition from tenants who documented every repair he skipped.
The opposition spent the whole session asking about the ferry contract and got the same non-answer eleven times.
Our striker spent the first half studying the opposition goalkeeper, then chipped him from the edge of the box.
She expected opposition from the finance team and instead got a shrug and a signature within the hour.

meanings.en: to prevent someone's plan or crime from succeeding
very thin flexible metal sheeting, used especially for wrapping or covering food
a person or thing that contrasts with another and makes the other's qualities more noticeable

examples: A jammed fire door foiled the thieves, who abandoned two laptops in the stairwell and left through the kitchen.
Their plan to surprise her at the airport was foiled by a delayed connection and a phone at four percent.
He wrapped the leftover salmon in foil and forgot it in the office fridge until the smell became everyone's problem.
Line the tray with foil first, unless you enjoy scrubbing burnt marinade off metal for twenty minutes.
The quiet accountant works as a foil to his loud brother, and audiences notice the contrast within one scene.

meanings.en: a person who publicly argues in favour of an idea, policy or course of action

examples: The loudest proponent of the four-day week turned out to be the manager who tracked everyone's login times.
Proponents of the new cycle lane packed the council meeting, and the objectors arrived twenty minutes after the vote.
As a proponent of open-plan offices she now works from a cupboard she describes as a focus room.
Early proponents of the vaccine schedule spent years answering the same three questions at community halls.
He remains a proponent of writing tests first, even on the weekend projects nobody else will ever read.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + ponere(放置) → 提出主张的人

meanings.en: lasting only a short time; not permanent
staying or working in a place for only a short period before moving on

examples: The relief was transient; twenty minutes after the painkiller wore off she was back on the clinic's waiting list.
Engineers traced the outage to a transient fault that never reappeared in six weeks of deliberate testing.
Ski towns build for a transient population, so half the apartments sit empty from April until the first snow.
His enthusiasm for running proved transient, and the expensive shoes now hold the bedroom door open.
The neighborhood has a transient feel, with new names on the buzzer roughly every eleven months.
words.etymology: trans-(穿过) + ire(走) → 走过就消失

meanings.en: full of interesting, important or exciting things happening
meanings.zh: 多事的;充满波折的;精彩纷呈的

examples: It was an eventful commute: a burst pipe, a replacement bus, and a stranger who insisted on sharing his sandwich.
Her first eventful week in the job included two resignations, a server fire, and a surprisingly calm all-hands meeting.
We wanted a quiet vacation and got an eventful one, complete with a lost passport and a very persuasive taxi driver.
The match was less eventful than the line outside, where two fans argued about a transfer that never happened.
After an eventful decade of moving cities, she now measures a good year by how little happens in it.

meanings.en: having a friendly, pleasant manner that is easy to like

examples: Our landlord is amiable on the phone and completely unreachable the moment the boiler actually stops working in February.
The interviewer kept things amiable for forty minutes, then asked the one question that had clearly decided everything.
He is an amiable presence in every standup, remembers your dog's name, and has never once shipped code on time.
The neighborhood group chat stayed amiable until someone proposed paid parking, and three people left within the hour.
Her amiable manner with customers hid a spreadsheet where every late supplier was ranked and quietly dropped.
words.etymology: amicus(朋友) + -abilis(可…的) → 和蔼可亲的

meanings.en: unpleasant to experience, smell, taste, or have to do
(of a person) bad-tempered and unfriendly to deal with

examples: Cleaning the office fridge in August is the most disagreeable task on the rota, and nobody ever volunteers twice.
The medicine works, but it leaves a disagreeable metallic taste that lingers through breakfast and most of the morning.
A disagreeable smell drifted from the vents all week before maintenance finally admitted a rat had died somewhere.
The building manager is so disagreeable on the phone that tenants now send emails and screenshot every reply.
Jet lag made him disagreeable at dinner, and he snapped at the waiter over a bread basket that arrived late.

meanings.en: in a way that is pleasant and gives enjoyment
in a way that shows willingness to agree or go along with something

examples: We were agreeably surprised by the rental: the photos undersold the balcony and nobody had mentioned the espresso machine.
The lecture hall was agreeably cool after the walk across campus, and half the front row fell asleep.
Dinner ended agreeably, with everyone splitting the bill by app and nobody arguing about who ordered the second bottle.
The first hour of the flight passed agreeably, until the toddler behind me discovered how loudly a tray table slams.
Asked to move the meeting an hour later, he shrugged agreeably and updated the invite before I finished explaining.

relatedForms.zh: 令人愉快的;欣然同意的

meanings.en: not honest; saying or doing things intended to cheat or mislead people

examples: The listing was dishonest about the commute: forty minutes door to door, but only if the train skipped four stops.
It felt dishonest to leave the five-star review up after the shop changed owners and quietly halved the portions.
Calling that chart a trend is intellectually dishonest when the axis starts at ninety and covers exactly three months.
He was not dishonest exactly, but his expense report described a taxi that had actually been a very long walk.
The bank flagged the application as dishonest once the payslips turned out to use a font released last year.

meanings.en: to deliberately make someone believe something that is not true
(of an appearance or one's senses) to give a false impression and mislead someone

examples: The startup deceived investors for two years with a demo video that had been filmed in one unusually lucky take.
She never lied outright; she simply let the timeline deceive everyone into thinking the funding had already arrived.
Do not let the quiet lobby deceive you — the clinic books three hundred appointments a day on the floors above.
Parents were deceived by an app that promised strict screen-time limits and quietly sold their children's location data.
He deceived himself into thinking the deadline was flexible until the client forwarded the signed contract on Friday morning.

relatedForms.zh: 欺骗性的;易使人误解的

words.etymology: de-(离开) + capere(抓住) → 使中圈套 → 欺骗

meanings.en: dishonest behaviour intended to make someone believe something that is not true

examples: The whole pitch rested on deceit: the demo video was edited to hide the four seconds the app took to load.
She forgave the missed anniversary but not the deceit, because he had spent a week rehearsing the alibi.
Auditors traced the deceit to a single spreadsheet where last quarter's numbers were quietly copied forward.
His resignation letter called it an error of judgment; the board minutes called it deceit and voted accordingly.
Dating apps run on small acts of deceit, from the height field to the photo taken nine years ago.
words.etymology: de-(离开) + capere(抓取) → 使人上当

meanings.en: feeling or showing shocked anger because something seems deeply unfair, offensive or morally wrong

examples: Parents were outraged that the school announced the fee increase two days before the payment deadline.
The comment section filled with outraged strangers who had clearly read only the headline of the article.
He sounded outraged on the call, then admitted afterwards that he had approved the very same policy in March.
Long-time subscribers were outraged when the streaming service quietly deleted the shows they had already paid for.
An outraged email from one resident forced the council to publish the traffic data it had been sitting on.
words.etymology: ultra(超出) + -age → 过分之举 → 激起愤慨

meanings.en: offended and slightly angry because someone has been rude to you or has treated you without respect

examples: The chef looked affronted when a diner asked for ketchup before tasting a single bite of the dish.
She was affronted less by the rejection than by the template email that misspelled her name twice.
My grandmother seemed genuinely affronted that we booked a restaurant instead of eating the dumplings she had frozen.
He walked out of the meeting affronted, having been asked to summarize a project he had personally led for years.
The cat sat by the empty bowl with an affronted expression, as though breakfast were a legal entitlement.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + frons(额头,脸) → 当面顶撞 → 冒犯

meanings.en: feeling bitter and angry about something you consider unfair, often for a long time afterwards
meanings.zh: 愤恨的;怨恨的;心怀不满的

examples: She grew resentful of the colleague who presented her slides to the client and never mentioned her name.
Six months of covering his shifts left the whole night team quietly resentful and unusually slow to volunteer.
He is resentful that his brother inherited the flat, though he refused to visit their mother for years.
New hires became resentful once they saw the salary bands the job ad had promised to publish openly.
A resentful silence settled over dinner the moment someone mentioned who had actually paid for the holiday.
words.etymology: re-(反复) + sentire(感觉) → 反复回味 → 怨恨

meanings.en: a feeling of bitter anger about something unfair that you cannot forget or forgive

examples: Years of unpaid overtime built a quiet resentment that surfaced only in the anonymous engagement survey.
The promotion went to the newest hire, and the resentment in the team chat was audible even in emoji.
Splitting the bill evenly every Friday created more resentment than anyone was willing to say out loud.
She carried a low hum of resentment toward the sister who moved abroad and left the caregiving behind.
The landlord's third rent increase turned polite complaints into open resentment at the residents' meeting.
words.etymology: re-(反复) + sentire(感觉) → 反复回味 → 怨恨

meanings.en: changing often and without good reason, especially in loyalties, preferences or affections
meanings.zh: 变化无常的;易变心的;靠不住的

examples: Streaming audiences are fickle: the show topped the charts in April and vanished from every recommendation row by June.
London weather in spring is fickle enough that she carries sunglasses and an umbrella in the same tote bag.
Our biggest client is fickle about branding, approving the blue logo on Monday and demanding green by Thursday afternoon.
He blamed his fickle appetite on the new medication, though the kitchen suspected the delivery app's endless menu.
Investors proved fickle once interest rates moved, pulling out of the fund they had praised at the conference.

meanings.en: a sudden change of mood or behaviour with no sensible reason behind it; an impulsive whim
meanings.zh: 反复无常;一时兴起;任性的念头

examples: The rota changed again on Friday, and nobody could tell whether it followed a policy or the manager's caprice.
Startup salaries here rise and fall on the caprice of two investors who have never met the engineering team.
She redesigned the entire homepage on a caprice, then spent the weekend restoring the version her users preferred.
Farmers cannot plan around the caprices of a monsoon that arrives three weeks early one year and never the next.
Promotions at that firm depended less on results than on the caprice of whoever happened to chair the review.
words.etymology: capo(头) + riccio(刺猬) → 毛发竖起 → 突发奇想

meanings.en: attracting attention by looking expensive, bright or showy, often in a tasteless way or without real substance behind it
meanings.zh: 浮华的;炫耀的;华而不实的

examples: He arrived in a flashy rented convertible, which the client's parking attendant photographed before anyone had shaken hands.
The pitch deck was flashy, full of animated transitions, but the revenue slide had been quietly left out.
Her code review flagged a flashy one-line solution and asked for the boring version the next maintainer could read.
Recruiters warned him that a flashy watch in an interview reads differently in Zurich than it does in Dubai.
The club signed a flashy winger and spent the season wishing they had bought a defensive midfielder instead.

meanings.en: very rich, elaborate or luxurious; produced or provided in unusually generous amounts
to give money, praise or attention to someone or something in very generous, even excessive, amounts
meanings.zh: 慷慨给予;大量倾注;挥霍

examples: The company threw a lavish launch party in November and cut the entire marketing team by early February.
Her grandmother's lavish Sunday lunches ran to four courses, and nobody was allowed to leave before the fruit.
Reviewers praised the film's lavish costumes while noting that the script fits comfortably on a single index card.
He lavished attention on the landing page and forgot that the checkout button had been broken for days.
Critics lavished praise on the debut album, and the band spent three years failing to repeat it.
words.etymology: lavare(洗) → lavasse(倾盆大雨) → 挥霍、奢华

meanings.en: appealing to the senses of sight, sound, touch, taste or smell, especially in a way that gives aesthetic pleasure
meanings.zh: 感官的;悦人感官的;给人美感享受的

examples: The perfume counter aims for a sensuous experience, though at nine in the morning it mostly smells overwhelming.
Wood, wool and unglazed clay give the reading room a sensuous warmth that the previous glass box lacked.
She writes about food in sensuous detail, so readers finish the column hungry and slightly annoyed about it.
The cellist drew a slow, sensuous line from the low strings while the hall's air conditioning hummed along.
Designers chose a sensuous curve for the handle, and testers held the kettle longer than the task required.
words.etymology: sensus(感觉) + -ous → 诉诸感官的

meanings.en: avoiding a direct answer or a clear commitment, often deliberately
meanings.zh: 含糊其辞的;回避问题的

meanings.en: done in order to avoid something dangerous or unwanted

examples: His answers in the standup were so evasive that three people privately messaged the same question afterward.
The landlord stayed evasive about the mold until an inspector arrived with a moisture meter and a clipboard.
She gave an evasive smile when asked whether the layoffs were finished, then steered the meeting toward catering.
The cyclist took evasive action when a delivery van drifted into the bike lane without signaling once.
Our pilot made one sharp evasive turn around the storm cell, and every tray table rattled for a minute.
words.etymology: e-(出) + vadere(走) → 躲开

meanings.en: to officially cancel a law, decision, offer, or agreement so that it no longer has force

examples: The startup rescinded her offer two days before her start date, citing a hiring freeze nobody had mentioned.
After the parking backlash, the council rescinded the new permit rules and quietly refunded everyone who had paid.
Management rescinded the four-day week within a quarter, blaming a productivity dashboard nobody outside finance had ever seen.
If the buyer misses the deposit deadline, the seller can rescind the contract without paying any penalty.
The university rescinded his admission after the essay he submitted turned up, nearly word for word, on a blog.
words.etymology: re-(回) + scindere(切开) → 撤销

meanings.en: widely known and publicly praised for a particular quality or achievement

examples: The celebrated pastry chef now runs a six-seat counter above a laundromat and takes bookings only by postcard.
Our department hired a celebrated researcher who turned out to be hopeless at email and brilliant at everything else.
That celebrated opening paragraph gets quoted in every writing workshop, usually by someone who never finished the novel.
The museum's most celebrated painting hangs in a small side room, guarded by one bored attendant and a rope.
Her celebrated debut album still outsells everything she has released since, which she mentions in interviews with visible patience.

meanings.en: well known and greatly respected because of a long record of impressive achievements
meanings.zh: 杰出的;卓越的;声名显赫的

examples: The lab's illustrious founder still shows up on Fridays to argue about coffee filters and, occasionally, about physics.
She joined an illustrious line of city planners whose bike lanes were ridiculed for a decade and then copied everywhere.
His illustrious career ended with a podcast about sourdough, which he insists is the most honest work he has done.
The conference booked an illustrious keynote speaker, then scheduled him against the free lunch and wondered why attendance collapsed.
Behind the counter hangs a photo of the diner's illustrious first customer, a mayor nobody under forty can name.
words.etymology: il-(使) + lustrare(照亮) → 显赫的

meanings.en: the state of being widely known and admired, especially for a skill or achievement

examples: Her renown in the neighborhood rests entirely on a chili recipe she refuses to write down for anyone.
The bakery's renown spread through one viral video, and now the queue starts before the ovens are even warm.
He traded academic renown for a quiet consultancy, and says the only thing he misses is free library access.
Winning that design prize brought the studio international renown and, less romantically, three years of unbearable email volume.
The town's renown as a birding destination collapsed after the wetland was drained for a distribution warehouse.
words.etymology: re-(反复) + nomer(命名) → 名声

meanings.en: to say very strongly and usually publicly that something or someone is wrong or unacceptable
meanings.zh: 谴责;强烈批评;公开抨击

meanings.en: to sentence someone to a punishment, or to force someone into a situation they cannot escape
meanings.zh: 判处(刑罚);使注定遭受(不幸)

meanings.en: to declare officially that a building or structure is unsafe and unfit to be used
meanings.zh: 宣布(建筑物)不适合使用;判定为危房

examples: The foreign ministry condemned the missile strike within an hour, though the statement carefully avoided naming the country responsible.
Alumni condemned the university's decision to rename the scholarship after a donor whose company had just settled a wage-theft lawsuit.
A single missed diagnosis condemned him to eighteen months of appointments, and the clinic still insists its intake form was clear.
The city condemned the flooded apartment block on Tuesday, giving forty tenants six days to find somewhere else to sleep.
Her podcast condemns the influencer economy in one breath and sells a sixty-dollar skincare bundle in the next.

relatedForms.zh: 被判刑的;被判定危险的

words.etymology: con-(加强) + damnare(判罚) → 判罪 → 谴责

meanings.en: feeling worried or uneasy about something whose outcome is uncertain
very much wanting something to happen, often with a trace of nervousness

examples: Parents grew anxious as the school app stayed silent for three hours after the bus was rerouted around the flooded underpass.
He gets anxious before every performance review, rehearsing answers in the stairwell until his manager finally opens the meeting room.
Anxious about the wildfire smoke, she checked the air-quality index four times before letting the children walk to practice.
The startup is anxious to announce the funding round, but legal wants two more days with the term sheet.
Anxious to prove herself, the new resident volunteered for the night shift during her first week on the ward.
words.etymology: angere(勒紧;窒息) + -ous → 心被勒紧 → 焦虑的

meanings.en: to catch and arrest someone suspected of a crime
to understand or grasp something, especially something abstract or difficult
meanings.zh: 领会;理解(尤指抽象事物)

examples: Two officers apprehended the suspect in a parking garage six blocks from the jewelry store, still carrying the pry bar.
The fugitive was apprehended at passport control after a border agent noticed the photograph had been printed on ordinary paper.
Store security apprehended the man reselling stolen scooters, then waited forty minutes for a patrol car on a busy Friday.
Readers can apprehend the scale of the deficit only when the report converts it into hospitals that were never built.
Nobody in the meeting fully apprehended what the merger would mean until the new org chart appeared on the second slide.
words.etymology: ad-(朝向) + prehendere(抓住) → 抓住 → 逮捕;领会

meanings.en: following a course full of bends and turns rather than running straight, literally or figuratively

examples: The bus took a winding mountain road to the trailhead, and three passengers spent the last hour staring hard at the horizon.
Her apartment sits at the top of a winding staircase that makes every grocery delivery a negotiation with the courier.
The refugee's winding route to citizenship took eleven years, four lawyers, and a filing cabinet of documents she still keeps.
A winding queue of fans wrapped around the arena, doubling back twice past the merchandise tents before reaching the gate.
The river's winding channel has shifted a hundred meters since the 1980s survey, so the county redrew the property lines.

meanings.en: so bad or offensive that it deserves strong public condemnation
meanings.zh: 应受谴责的;可耻的;糟糕透顶的

meanings.en: extremely poor in quality or condition, in a way that shocks or dismays

examples: The referee called the crowd's chanting deplorable and threatened to suspend the match until the stewards cleared the north stand.
Screenshots showed the manager mocking an employee's disability, behavior the company called deplorable in a statement issued the same night.
Inspectors found deplorable conditions in the meat plant: standing water, a broken chiller, and rodent droppings near the packing line.
The rental was advertised as cozy, but the deplorable state of the wiring made the electrician refuse to switch anything on.
Fans called the club's response deplorable, since the apology arrived eight days late and misspelled the injured player's name.
words.etymology: de-(彻底) + plorare(哭喊) → 值得痛哭 → 糟糕透顶

meanings.en: shockingly unfair, offensive or excessive, so that people react with anger
meanings.zh: 骇人听闻的;令人愤慨的;离谱过分的

meanings.en: strikingly bold or unconventional, often in a way that entertains rather than offends
meanings.zh: 惊世骇俗的;夸张出格的;大胆吸睛的

examples: Tenants called the 40 percent rent increase outrageous and packed the council meeting until the landlord's lawyer left early.
The comedian built the whole set on outrageous impressions of her own relatives, three of whom were sitting in row four.
Charging nine dollars for a bottle of water at the airport gate feels outrageous even to travelers who expect it.
The audit uncovered outrageous expense claims, including a jet ski logged as team-building equipment for a two-person marketing department.
She wore an outrageous neon-green suit to the ceremony and dominated every photo gallery published the next morning.
words.etymology: outre(超出) + -age → 越出常轨 → 骇人的

meanings.en: a public statement in which someone strongly criticizes or condemns a person, action or idea as wrong or evil

examples: Her three-minute denunciation of the pension cuts drew louder applause than anything else at the union conference.
The company answered the leaked emails with a flat denunciation of the reporter rather than a single factual correction.
What began as a routine product review turned into a denunciation of the entire subscription model, and the video hit two million views.
The bishop's denunciation of the loan scheme was read aloud in every parish that Sunday morning.
Neighbours expected sympathy at the residents' meeting and got a denunciation of the landlord's twelve-year record of ignored repairs.
words.etymology: de-(向下) + nuntiare(宣告) → 当众宣告罪状 → 谴责

meanings.en: to support or strengthen an argument, position or system by providing evidence or extra backing
meanings.zh: 支持;加强;支撑(论点、地位等)

meanings.en: a stone or brick structure built against a wall to hold it up; anything that gives strong support
meanings.zh: 扶壁;拱扶垛;支柱;支撑物

examples: The startup buttressed its valuation with three years of subscriber data instead of the usual slide about market size.
Prosecutors buttressed the timeline with door-camera footage, and the defence stopped arguing about when the van arrived.
Cheap parking has long buttressed the mall's weekend traffic, which is why the new fee terrified every tenant.
Scaffolding now hides the cathedral's north buttress while masons replace stone that has been crumbling since the 1970s.
Her grandmother's pension is the quiet buttress of the household, covering the rent whenever the restaurant has a slow month.

meanings.en: not faithful to a person, group, or country that one owes support to; betraying trust
meanings.zh: 不忠的;不忠诚的;背信弃义的

examples: Forwarding the salary spreadsheet to a rival firm struck the partners as disloyal, and she was walked out before lunch.
He felt vaguely disloyal buying groceries at the new chain while the corner shop that had extended him credit sat empty.
The manager called the striker disloyal for liking a transfer rumour on Instagram, which only made the story bigger.
Nobody thought the leak was disloyal until the memo showed the whistleblower had also been paid by the contractor.
Switching to her sister's wedding photographer felt disloyal, though the old one had raised his prices twice that year.

meanings.en: to disagree with a plan, policy or person and try actively to stop or change it

examples: Residents opposed the data centre at three consecutive council meetings, arguing about water use rather than noise.
She opposes the four-day week her own union negotiated, saying the compressed shifts will land hardest on night nurses.
Two board members opposed the merger, and their dissent was recorded in a footnote nobody read until the lawsuit.
Teachers who oppose the phone ban say confiscating handsets simply moves the argument into the corridor.
The pharmacy chain is opposing the refund rule in court, though its own survey showed customers wanted it.
words.etymology: ob-(对面) + ponere(放置) → 放在对立面 → 反对

meanings.en: weakened or damaged so that something no longer works as well as it should, especially a bodily function or ability
meanings.zh: 受损的;功能减弱的;(身体机能)有障碍的

examples: The station's new announcements were designed for visually impaired passengers, who had been complaining about the silent departure screens.
Two nights of four-hour sleep left his judgement so impaired that he approved the invoice without opening the attachment.
Insurers argued the driver was impaired by prescription medication, not alcohol, which changed the entire structure of the claim.
Her hearing has been impaired since the concert, and she now watches every film at home with subtitles on.
Flood damage left the bridge structurally impaired, so lorries have been detoured through the village for eleven months.

meanings.en: a condition in which a physical or mental function is weakened or damaged, or the process of such weakening

examples: The school added a quiet room after a survey found sensory impairments among more pupils than anyone had assumed.
His cognitive impairment shows up first in cooking: the recipe he made weekly for decades now takes two hours.
The bank reported a large impairment on its commercial property loans, and the share price fell before the call ended.
Airlines must record any impairment that affects a pilot's vision, even one corrected fully by ordinary glasses.
Long shifts under headphones produced measurable hearing impairment in warehouse staff, according to the audit published last spring.

meanings.en: the quality of speaking honestly and directly, even when the truth is unwelcome or awkward

examples: Her frankness in the exit interview startled HR: she named the three managers whose meetings had made the whole team quit.
The startup founder answered investor questions with a frankness rare in pitch decks, admitting the app had lost users for six straight months.
Doctors are trained to balance frankness with kindness, telling patients the prognosis plainly without stripping away every reason to hope.
I appreciated his frankness about salary bands, since most recruiters dodge the number until the fourth call of the process.
The memoir's frankness about her divorce cost her several friendships but earned it a place on every book club list.

meanings.en: to express sympathy to someone who is unhappy or unlucky, often by sharing that you feel the same way

examples: After the layoffs were announced, the two engineers commiserated over cheap noodles and traded links to job boards.
Fans of the losing team commiserated in the group chat until three in the morning, replaying the missed penalty frame by frame.
She called her sister to commiserate about their mother's hospital paperwork, which had been rejected twice for the same missing signature.
New parents commiserate about sleep the way commuters complain about trains: constantly, and with a strange kind of pride.
I stopped by his desk to commiserate after the client killed the redesign he had spent four months building.
words.etymology: com-(共同) + miser(苦难) → 共感苦难 → 同情

meanings.en: feeling resentful because you believe you have been treated unfairly
meanings.zh: 感到委屈的;愤愤不平的;感到受冤的

meanings.en: having suffered a legal wrong, and therefore entitled to bring a complaint or claim
meanings.zh: (法律上)受损害的;权利受侵害的

examples: He left the performance review looking aggrieved, convinced that his rating had been lowered to fund someone else's promotion.
Aggrieved season-ticket holders filled the club's inbox after the owner raised prices and sold the two best players in one week.
She sounded genuinely aggrieved that nobody had told her the deadline moved, though the change sat in a thread she had muted.
Under the statute, any aggrieved employee may file a complaint with the labour board within one hundred and eighty days.
The court allowed the aggrieved tenants to join a single suit against the landlord who had ignored three years of repair orders.
words.etymology: ad-(加于) + gravis(沉重) → 加以重压 → 受委屈

meanings.en: quietly happy and satisfied with what you have, without wanting anything more
meanings.zh: 满足的;心满意足的;安心的

examples: Six months after leaving the consulting job, he seemed genuinely contented, teaching two classes and cycling home before dark.
The cat lay in the one patch of afternoon sun on the office floor, contented and entirely indifferent to our deployment crisis.
She is contented with a modest flat and a short commute, which baffles colleagues who measure success in square metres.
The survey found nurses on the new rota were more contented than those working the old twelve-hour night shifts.
My grandfather looked contented in the wedding photos, holding a paper cup and letting everyone else make the speeches.

meanings.en: willing to hurt or ignore other people in order to get what you want, showing no pity
meanings.zh: 无情的;残酷的;冷酷无情的

meanings.en: rigorous and unsparing in a way that is admired, especially in cutting away what is not needed
meanings.zh: 毫不留情的;严格彻底的(常含褒义)

examples: The new owner was ruthless with costs, closing two warehouses and cancelling the pensions review before his first month ended.
Chinese e-commerce is ruthless in December: a seller who misses the shipping window loses the ranking slot for the whole quarter.
Be ruthless when packing for a week in Tokyo — every extra jumper costs you space you will want for books.
Her editor was ruthless with the opening chapter, cutting forty pages of backstory and telling her to start at the funeral.
The product team was ruthless about scope, stripping every feature under two percent usage so the launch finally shipped on schedule.

meanings.en: the state of being first in importance, order or rank, above everything else of its kind

examples: The ruling reaffirmed the primacy of the written contract over whatever the sales team had promised on the phone.
Streaming has not ended the primacy of the cinema opening weekend, which still decides how a studio funds its next film.
Engineers argued for hours about the primacy of speed over accuracy, until the medical client settled it in one sentence.
The bank's memo insisted on the primacy of the Shanghai office, and three directors quietly began looking for new roles.
Her thesis questions the primacy of grammar drills in language teaching, citing classrooms where nobody could order a coffee.
words.etymology: primus(第一) + -acy(状态) → 居首之位 → 首要地位

meanings.en: inclined to argue and disagree with people, often about small or petty things
meanings.zh: 爱争吵的;好争辩的;爱抬杠的

examples: Two quarrelsome neighbours turned the building's group chat into a nightly argument about which bins belonged to whom.
The panel show hires quarrelsome guests on purpose, because polite agreement never trends and viewers stay for the shouting.
My grandfather grows quarrelsome after his second whisky, relitigating a 1987 property dispute that everyone else has long forgotten.
Standups grew quarrelsome once two teams shared one backlog, and the manager started scheduling them in separate rooms.
Rescue volunteers warned us the older cat was quarrelsome with other pets, so she now rules the apartment alone.
words.etymology: queri(抱怨) + -some(易…的) → 爱争吵的

meanings.en: done or happening because of a sudden impulse, without being planned or arranged in advance
meanings.zh: 自发的;即兴的;一时冲动的

meanings.en: occurring naturally, without an obvious external cause or any deliberate effort
meanings.zh: 自然发生的;非人为的;不由自主的

examples: We made a spontaneous decision at the station and took the slow train to Bruges instead of going home.
Her resignation speech drew spontaneous applause from a newsroom that had spent three months rehearsing its silence.
Dating apps have made spontaneous evenings rare; nobody meets anyone now without two weeks of scheduling and a confirmation text.
The warehouse fire was traced to spontaneous combustion in a pallet of oily rags left beside the loading dock.
Most of these tumours undergo spontaneous regression, the oncologist said, so we are monitoring the scan rather than operating this month.
words.etymology: sponte(自愿) → 出于本意 → 自发的

meanings.en: to defeat or gain control of someone by using greater strength or force
(of a smell, taste or feeling) to be so strong that it overwhelms everything else
meanings.zh: (气味、味道、情绪)盖过;压过;使难以忍受

examples: Two staff members overpowered the man at the gate before police arrived, and the concert restarted twenty minutes late.
The suspect overpowered a security guard in the hospital corridor and was arrested three streets away that same night.
Wolves rarely overpower a healthy adult elk, so the pack targets the animals limping at the back of the herd.
Truffle oil overpowers everything on the plate, which is why the chef now keeps one bottle locked in his office.
The smell of fresh paint overpowered us the moment we opened the flat, and we spent the evening on the balcony.

relatedForms.zh: 强烈的;压倒性的;令人难以抗拒的

meanings.en: relating to or involved in a secret plan by a group to do something harmful or illegal
meanings.zh: 阴谋的;密谋的;搞阴谋论的

meanings.en: (of a look, smile or voice) suggesting that you are sharing a secret with someone
meanings.zh: (神情、语气)心照不宣的;像是有秘密的

examples: The podcast slid from health advice into conspiratorial territory, and two sponsors quietly pulled their ads within a fortnight.
Moderators say conspiratorial posts spike after every power cut, blaming everything from the utility company to the weather satellites.
Prosecutors described a conspiratorial group chat in which the three traders coordinated their bids months before the auction closed.
She leaned across the desk with a conspiratorial whisper and told me which manager was actually leaving in March.
