The barista gave me a conspiratorial grin and slid an extra pastry into the bag, mouthing that it was yesterday's.

relatedForms.zh: 心照不宣地;像密谋般地

words.etymology: con-(共同) + spirare(呼吸) → 同气相通 → 密谋的

meanings.en: confused and unable to understand something, and usually showing it in your face or voice
meanings.zh: 困惑的;迷惑不解的;摸不着头脑的

examples: She read the invoice twice, puzzled by a delivery charge for an address she had never lived at.
The vet looked puzzled: the X-ray showed nothing, yet the dog had refused to climb stairs for a week.
Puzzled tourists gathered under the departure board, where every flight to Lisbon had been replaced by a blinking dash.
My father sent a puzzled voice note asking why the banking app now wanted his face instead of a password.
Half the class still looked puzzled after the third explanation, so the teacher abandoned the slides and drew the diagram again.

relatedForms.zh: 令人费解的;莫名其妙的

meanings.en: having or showing a rational, tolerant and well-informed outlook, free from prejudice or superstition
meanings.zh: 开明的;有见识的;文明进步的

meanings.en: having attained deep spiritual insight or awakening

examples: The company calls its four-day week enlightened, though it began as a desperate attempt to stop senior engineers resigning.
Compared with its neighbours, the city has an enlightened housing policy: deposits are capped and evictions require a genuine reason.
My grandmother was unusually enlightened for her generation, sending three daughters to university when the village expected early marriages.
Museums now describe their old collecting practices as anything but enlightened, and several galleries have begun returning objects to Nigeria.
The retreat's website promises an enlightened teacher, but the reviews mostly praise the vegetarian breakfast and the silence after nine.

meanings.en: so slight or delicate that it is hard to notice or describe
meanings.zh: 微妙的;细微的;不易察觉的

meanings.en: clever and indirect, achieving an effect without being obvious about it
meanings.zh: 巧妙的;含蓄的;不动声色的

examples: The redesign made only subtle changes to the checkout page, yet returning customers noticed the cart button had shifted left.
A subtle burnt note in the espresso told the barista her new grinder was running hotter than the shop's old one.
The MRI showed a subtle shadow the radiologist almost skipped, and the follow-up scan two weeks later confirmed her caution.
Her resignation email was a subtle piece of work, thanking the department warmly while making the reason for leaving unmistakable.
The campaign's messaging was anything but subtle, plastering the candidate's face across every bus shelter in the district.
words.etymology: sub-(在下) + tela(织物) → 织得细密 → 微妙的

meanings.en: willing to consider ideas, evidence or ways of living that differ from your own
meanings.zh: 思想开明的;虚心的;不抱成见的

examples: The hiring panel stayed open-minded about candidates without degrees, and their strongest new engineer had learned everything at a community bootcamp.
My grandmother is surprisingly open-minded about technology, video-calling her friends in Chengdu every Sunday and asking me about translation apps.
Come to the tasting open-minded: the chef pairs oysters with green apple sorbet, and diners who arrive skeptical usually leave converted.
The city council promised to be open-minded about the bike-lane proposal, then scheduled the only public hearing for a Tuesday morning.
Living in three countries before thirty made him open-minded about how families work, though he still refuses to eat breakfast standing up.

meanings.en: willing to agree to something or be persuaded by it, rather than resisting
meanings.zh: 愿意接受的;顺从的;好说话的

examples: The landlord proved amenable to a shorter lease once she learned the tenant worked nights and would never park in the driveway.
Our vendor is amenable to monthly invoicing, which finally lets the finance team close the books without three days of chasing receipts.
The toddler was amenable to bedtime only after the third story, and only if the hallway light stayed on.
Negotiators found the union amenable to a phased raise, provided the company dropped its plan to outsource weekend shifts.
Ask him before lunch: he is far more amenable to schedule changes when the morning's inbox has not yet buried him.
words.etymology: a-(向) + mener(带领) → 可被引导 → 愿意接受的

meanings.en: friendly and easy to talk to, especially despite holding authority or status
meanings.zh: 平易近人的;和蔼可亲的

meanings.en: easy to understand or enjoy without special training or knowledge
meanings.zh: 易懂的;门槛低的;平实易读的

examples: The new principal is approachable in a way her predecessor never was, eating lunch in the cafeteria and learning every seventh-grader's name.
Patients rate the clinic highly because its doctors stay approachable, answering follow-up questions by message instead of booking another appointment.
He looks intimidating on stage, but backstage he was completely approachable, signing setlists and asking the opening band about their van.
The book makes quantum computing approachable, trading equations for a running analogy about coins spinning on a kitchen table.
Junior staff avoid the finance director, though her deputy is approachable enough that half the building routes questions through him.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + prope(近) → 靠近 → 平易近人的

meanings.en: unwilling to consider ideas or evidence that conflict with what you already believe
meanings.zh: 思想封闭的;固执己见的;听不进意见的

examples: The committee's closed-minded response to the pilot data killed a program three other districts adopted the following year.
He is not stupid, just closed-minded about anything invented after 1995, which makes onboarding him to the new CRM a weekly ordeal.
Reviewers called the documentary closed-minded for interviewing eleven opponents of the housing plan and not a single resident who supported it.
Growing up in a closed-minded town taught her to keep her sketchbook hidden until she reached art school in another province.
Calling a colleague closed-minded in a design review ends the conversation faster than any argument about the actual interface.

meanings.en: showing that you think someone or something is not worth serious attention
meanings.zh: 轻蔑的;不屑一顾的;敷衍了事的

examples: The reply was three words and dismissive, so she forwarded her proposal to a manager who actually reads attachments.
Critics were dismissive of the debut album in 2019 and quietly rewrote their lists when it went platinum three years later.
Her doctor was dismissive of the fatigue for two years before a blood test finally found the thyroid problem behind it.
He waved a dismissive hand at the safety checklist, and the inspector wrote that gesture into the report verbatim.
The minister's dismissive shrug on live television trended for a week and cost her party more support than the policy itself.
words.etymology: dis-(离开) + mittere(送) → 送走 → 不屑一顾的

meanings.en: not reacting or replying to what someone says, asks for or needs
meanings.zh: 不回应的;反应冷淡的;置之不理的

meanings.en: of a machine, program or control, failing to react to input so that it appears frozen or broken
meanings.zh: 无响应的;失灵的;卡死的

examples: Three days after the interview, the hiring manager went unresponsive, leaving four candidates refreshing an inbox that never filled.
The landlord stayed unresponsive to every message about the broken boiler until the tenants filed a complaint with the council.
The checkout page froze halfway through the sale, and the payment button sat unresponsive while carts quietly emptied across three time zones.
Her two-year-old laptop turns unresponsive whenever the video call and the spreadsheet run together, so she closes one before opening the other.
The committee remained unresponsive to student petitions for a second year, so the union organized a sit-in outside the registrar's office.
words.etymology: un-(不) + re-(回) + spondere(应答) → 不作回应

meanings.en: the capacity of a person, group or system to take in new ideas, messages or influences, treated as a measurable general condition
meanings.zh: 接受能力;接纳程度;感受性

examples: The survey measured consumer receptivity to subscription pricing across six markets, and Brazil scored nearly twice as high as Germany.
Her dissertation argues that adolescent receptivity to political messaging peaks in the months just before a first election, then declines sharply.
Diplomats read Beijing's silence as a signal of low receptivity, and the draft climate language was quietly softened before the next round.
The lab tests whether sleep deprivation reduces receptivity to unfamiliar sounds, playing tone sequences to volunteers who have been awake nineteen hours.
Venture partners talk about market receptivity the way farmers talk about rainfall: you can time a launch around it but never command it.
words.etymology: re-(回) + capere(取) → 接纳 → 接受能力

meanings.en: a person's willingness to listen to and seriously consider other people's ideas, feelings or suggestions
meanings.zh: 乐于接受;愿意倾听;虚心

examples: What surprised her about the new manager was his receptiveness: he asked for the criticism first and thanked the intern who gave it.
My father's receptiveness to the idea of moving closer to us grew only after his second winter alone with the driveway.
The coach praised the team's receptiveness at halftime, when four players actually changed position instead of arguing with the whiteboard.
He mistook politeness for receptiveness, and only realized his pitch had failed when the investor's assistant sent a two-line email that Friday.
Couples therapy did not fix the arguments, but it gave both of them enough receptiveness to let the other finish a sentence.

relatedForms.zh: 乐于接受的;愿意倾听的

words.etymology: re-(回) + capere(取) → 接纳 → 乐于接受

meanings.en: a process in which a neutral third party helps two sides in a dispute talk and reach a voluntary settlement without going to court
action or a gesture intended to calm anger and win back goodwill from an opponent

examples: The union agreed to conciliation before striking, and an officer spent two days shuttling between the depot canteen and the management office.
Kenya's electoral commission opened conciliation talks with the opposition after three weeks of protests closed the main road into Nairobi.
Their divorce went through conciliation instead of court, which saved eleven months and let the children keep the same school year.
Under the platform's new terms, sellers must attempt conciliation with a mediator before any refund dispute reaches a tribunal.
His speech was pure conciliation: praise for the rival faction, an apology for the leaked memo, and no mention of the vote count.
words.etymology: con-(共同) + calare(召唤) → 召集一处 → 调解

meanings.en: the settling of a dispute by an independent person or panel whose decision both sides agree in advance to accept, used instead of a court trial

examples: The two shipping firms sent their cargo dispute to arbitration in Singapore, and the award landed eleven months faster than a London trial.
Buried on page nine, the app's terms force every user into arbitration, quietly stripping the right to join a class action.
Baseball salary arbitration gave the pitcher his asking figure, and the club's payroll rose by four million dollars before opening day.
A mining company won arbitration against the government over a canceled permit, and the ruling now hangs over the country's borrowing costs.
Their construction contract sends delay claims to arbitration, so the subcontractor's lawyers spent August assembling site photographs instead of drafting a lawsuit.
words.etymology: arbiter(裁判;见证人) → 第三方裁决 → 仲裁

meanings.en: the process of taking a dispute to court, including the lawsuits, filings and hearings it involves

examples: Years of patent litigation drained the startup's cash, and the founders sold the company to the very rival suing them.
The insurer settled quietly because litigation over the flooded warehouses would have opened its claims data to public inspection.
Climate litigation has moved from symbolic gestures to real risk: a Dutch court ordered one oil major to cut emissions outright.
Her whole first year at the firm was document review, the unglamorous engine room of litigation that no recruiting brochure mentions.
The homeowners' association threatened litigation over the neighbor's fence, then backed down when someone read the original 1998 deed.
words.etymology: lis(争端) + agere(进行) → 进行争讼 → 诉讼

meanings.en: to damage someone's reputation by saying or publishing something false about them

examples: The chef sued the reviewer for defaming her restaurant, claiming the food-poisoning allegation was invented and cost her two hundred bookings.
A viral thread defamed the wrong doctor, and the hospital spent a fortnight explaining that the man in the photograph had never worked there.
Under Singapore law, a politician can sue an ordinary citizen who defames him, and the damages have ended more than one career.
Her lawyer warned that repeating the rumor in the group chat could defame the former partner just as easily as printing it.
The energy firm accused campaigners of defaming its safety record, a claim the judge dismissed after seeing the inspection reports.
words.etymology: de-(损毁) + fama(名声) → 毁人名声 → 诽谤
